chapters.title: Fitt I — The Life and Death of Scyld
paragraphs:
Listen! We have heard of the glory of the Spear-Danes,
of the fame of those folk-kings in days gone by,
and how the princes performed deeds of valor.

Often Scyld Scefing tore away the mead-benches
from troops of enemies, from many a people.
Since first he was found friendless and wretched,
the warrior had known terror, but he found comfort for it.
He grew strong beneath the sky, gained honor in the world,
until all his neighbors across the sea were compelled
to bow to his command and bring him their tribute.
He was an excellent prince! Afterward a son was born to him,

a young heir in his household,
whom God the Father sent to comfort the people.
He had seen the misery malice had caused them,
how, deprived of their rulers, they had long
been wretched and afflicted. The Lord, in return,
the Wielder of Glory, blessed him with honor in the world.
Beowulf was famous — the glory of Scyld's great son
spread far and wide across the lands of the Danes.
So the young man, through kindnesses rendered
to his father's friends, with gifts in abundance,
must be able to earn, when old age approaches,
that eager companions will aid him in return,
and serve him as loyal warriors when war assaults him.
By praiseworthy actions must honor be won
among all the peoples. At the hour that was fated,

Scyld then departed, still warlike, into the keeping
of the All-Father. Away his loving comrades bore him
to the flowing tide, as he himself had commanded,
while the friend of the Scyldings wielded the power of words,
and the well-loved land-prince long had ruled them.
The ring-prowed vessel, the prince's ship,
lay there at anchor, icy and gleaming,
eager for its sailing. The beloved leader,
the giver of rings, they laid down there
on the breast of the ship, the famed one by the mainmast.
Many jewels, ornaments with fretted work,
brought from far lands, were placed near at hand.
I have never heard that a people furnished a ship
more splendidly with weapons of war, battle-gear,
swords and coats of mail. On his bosom sparkled
many a jewel that must travel with him
on the flood, far out upon the current.
They furnished him with no fewer gifts, with treasures
no less excellent, than those who first had sent him

outward at his birth, alone upon the sea,
the merest of infants. And they stretched a gold-wrought
standard high above his head beneath the sky,
let the sea-currents bear him, consigned him to the sea.
Their spirits were sad, their mood very mournful.
True men are not able,

those who dwell in halls, heroes under heaven,
to tell us for certain to what haven he came.

chapters.title: Fitt II — Scyld's Successors — Hrothgar's Great Mead-hall
paragraphs:
Then in the strongholds Beowulf, son of the Scyldings,
the beloved land-prince, was long famed among the people
(his father having departed, the prince from his dwelling),
until afterward great-minded Healfdene was born.
Throughout his life he graciously governed the Danes,
grim-minded and aged.

Four children, born in succession from his body,
woke in the world: that leader of warrior-troops
fathered Heorogar, Hrothgar, and Halga the good.
I heard that Elan was Ongentheow's consort,

the well-beloved bedmate of the War-Scylfing leader.
Then glory in battle was given to Hrothgar,
his war-fame grew so that his kinsmen willingly
obeyed his bidding, until the boys grew to manhood,
a numerous band. It burned in his spirit
to urge his people to build a great hall,
a mead-hall grander than men of that era

had ever heard of, and in it to share
with young and old all the blessings
the Lord had granted him — except life itself and his retainers.
Then the work, I find, was assigned far and wide
to many peoples across middle-earth's regions,
to adorn the great folk-hall. In due time it happened,
early among men, that it was entirely finished,
the greatest of hall-buildings. He named it Heorot,

he whose far-reaching word held sway among earls.
He did not break his promise; he lavished rings,
treasure at the banquet. The hall towered up
high and gable-crested, huge between its antler-like horns.
It awaited the waves of battle, the blasting fire-demon.
Before long, from the bitterest hatred, sword-wrath
would arise between a woman's husband and her father.
Then the mighty war-spirit endured for a season,

bore it bitterly, he who dwelt in darkness,
that loud, light-hearted laughter in the hall
greeted him daily. There was sweet harp-music,
the clear song of the singer. He who could do so said,

telling from ancient times of the beginnings of men,
that the Father Almighty had created the earth,
the fair fields that the water encircles,
and had set in triumph the beams of the sun and moon
to lavish their light on the land-folk and the races of men.
He adorned the earth in all its regions
with limbs and leaves; and He bestowed life as well
on all the kinds of creatures that live under heaven.

So blessed with abundance and brimming with joy
the warriors dwelt, until a certain one began
to hound them with deeds of direst malice —
a foe in the hall: this horrible stranger
was called Grendel, the famous march-stepper
who dwelt in the moor-fens, the marsh and the stronghold.
The gloomy-minded being had lived for a time
in the land of the giants, since the Lord and Creator
had banned and branded him. For that bitter murder,
the killing of Abel, the all-ruling Father

crushed the kindred of Cain with His vengeance.
He took no joy in the feud, but drove him far away
from kindred and kind, to atone for that crime,
the Measurer of Justice. From him came ill-favored creatures:
elves and giants, monsters of the ocean,
and the giants who long grappled with God.
He gave them their requital.

chapters.title: Fitt III — Grendel the Murderer
paragraphs:
When the sun had set, he set out to visit
the lofty hall, to see how the Ring-Danes had used it
for beds and benches once the banquet was over.
There he found many a noble reposing,
asleep after supper. The heroes knew
no sorrow, no misery. The evil monster,
greedy and cruel, tarried but little —

fierce and frenzied — and tore thirty thanes
from their slumber. Then he departed,
leaping and laughing, to return to his lair,
sallying homeward with a surfeit of slaughter.
In the dusk of dawning, just as day was breaking,
Grendel's prowess was revealed to the warriors:

then, his meal finished, a moan rose up,
a mighty morning-cry. The famous ruler,
the long-worthy prince, sat deep in grief,
suffered great sorrow, sighed for his warriors,
when they had seen the track of the hateful pursuer,
the accursed spirit — a sorrow too crushing,
too loathsome and lasting. Nor did he wait long,
for one night later he continued his slaughter,
shameless and shocking, shrinking but little
from malice and murder — they had so fully mastered him.
It was easy then to find men who looked elsewhere
for a pleasanter place to rest in the lodges,
a bed in the private chambers. When the hall-thane's hatred
was made known to them, shown by clear tokens,
he who had escaped the foe held himself after that
farther away and faster. So Grendel ruled
and strove against justice, alone against all men,
until the choicest of houses towered empty.

Long was that season: for twelve winters' time
the friend of the Scyldings suffered torture,
every affliction, endless agony. And so
it became certainly known to the children of men,
sadly told in verse, that Grendel long struggled
against Hrothgar. He cherished his grudges,
murderous malice, many a winter,
unremitting strife, and would by no means
wish to lift the life-woe from any warrior
of the Danish folk, nor settle for money.
No counselor could count for a moment
on handsome compensation at the murderer's hands.
The evil monster fiercely harassed them,
the ill-planning death-shadow, both elder and younger,
trapping and tricking them. He trod every night
the mist-covered moor-fens — men do not know
where witches and wizards wander and roam.
So the foe of mankind often accomplished
many grievous injuries, this horrible hermit;
he frequented Heorot, the gem-adorned palace,
once night had fallen

(though since God opposed him, he could not touch the throne,
the light-flashing jewel — he knew nothing of His love).
It was a fearful affliction to the friend of the Scyldings,

a soul-crushing sorrow. Not seldom in private
the king sat in council; they held conference
over what the brave should do against these unlooked-for terrors.
At the shrines of their idols they often promised
gifts and offerings, earnestly praying
that the devil from hell would help them lighten
their people's oppression. Such was the practice they used then,
the hope of the heathen. They remembered hell
in their innermost spirit; they did not know God,

the Judge of their actions, the All-wielding Ruler.
They could give no praise to the Guardian of Heaven,
the Wielder of Glory. Woe will be his
who through furious hatred drives his spirit
into the clutch of the fire; no comfort shall he find,
no growth in wisdom. Well for the man who,
living his life-days, may face his Lord
and find defense in his Father's embrace!

chapters.title: Fitt IV — Beowulf Goes to Hrothgar's Assistance
paragraphs:
So Healfdene's kinsman constantly brooded
on his long-lasting sorrow; the clever battle-thane
was not able in any way to escape these evils.
Too crushing was the sorrow that came upon the people,
loathsome and lasting the life-grinding torture,

the greatest of night-woes. Then Higelac's retainer,
a good man among the Geats, heard at home
of Grendel's deeds. Of heroes then living
he was the stoutest and strongest, sturdy and noble.
He ordered them to prepare a trusty ship;
he said he would seek the war-king over the ocean,
the noble folk-leader, since he needed warriors.
His wise companions chided him little
for the perilous venture, though they loved him dearly;
they urged the brave prince on, foretelling his glory.

The excellent knight from the people of the Geats
had selected retainers, those likeliest to prove
trustworthy warriors. With fourteen companions
he sought out the ship; a sea-crafty man
guided them to the edge of the country.
The days passed quickly; the ship was afloat,
the craft beneath the cliff. Well-equipped warriors
climbed up to the prow; the wave-currents twisted
the sea on the sand. The soldiers then carried
bright-shining jewels into the breast of the ship,
handsome war-armor. The heroes pushed off
the wooden ship on its wished-for adventure.

The foam-necked ship, driven by the breeze,
most like a bird, glided over the waters,
until twenty-four hours later
the curved-prow vessel had traveled such a distance
that the sailors saw the sloping embankments,
the sea cliffs gleaming, the steep mountains,
the enormous headlands. They were nearing land
at the end of the ocean. Up from there quickly
the men of the Weders climbed onto the mainland,
moored their vessel (battle-gear rattled,
mail-coats clattered), and thanked the Lord
that the way over the waters had been so gentle.
Then from high on the cliff edge the guard of the Scyldings,
whose duty it was to watch the sea-cliffs, saw
brave men carrying beautiful shields down the gangway,
their armor all ready. Anxiously he wondered,
musing over what men these could be.
High on his horse, Hrothgar's retainer
rode down to the coast, mightily brandished
the lance in his hand, and questioned them boldly:

"Who are you, mail-covered warriors
clad in your corslets, who have come driving
a high ship over the shoals of the waters,
and have hurried here beneath helmets across the ocean?
I have been the shore-guard, standing as warden
lest any enemies should ravage the Danish realm
with an army of warships. No warriors
have ever ventured more boldly to come here;
and I am sure you have had no approval from kinsmen,
no word of leave from your warriors.

Never have I seen a greater earl on earth
than one of your company — a hero in armor;
no low-ranking fellow merely adorned with weapons,
but — unless his looks deceive me — one of striking presence.
Now, before you go further on your journey
as treacherous spies into the land of the Scyldings,
I must know fully what race you belong to.
You far-away dwellers, you sea-faring sailors,
hear and heed my plain opinion:
it is most fitting for you to tell me quickly
from what place you have come."

chapters.title: Fitt V — The Geats Reach Heorot
paragraphs:
The chief of the strangers gave him answer,
the leader of the war-troop, and opened his word-hoard:

"We are sprung from the lineage of the Geatish people,
and we are hearth-companions of Higelac. My father,
a noble head-warrior called Ecgtheow, was known
to heroes beyond counting. Many a winter
he lived among the people before he passed on his journey,
old from his dwelling; every counselor across the world
well remembers him. We have come with kindly spirit
to visit your people's lord, the son of King Healfdene,
defender of the folk-troop. Be open in your counsel!
We bear a weighty message to the noble one,
the protector of the Danes — and, I think, we shall hide
nothing of our errand. You will know whether it is true,
as we heard tell, that some savage ravager,
some hidden stalker, on dark nights shows
an unheard-of hatred among the Danes
through the direst deeds, horrid destruction,
and the falling of the dead. With the least selfish intent

I am able to offer counsel to Hrothgar,
how he, wise and worthy, may overcome the destroyer,
if the anguish of sorrow is ever to be lessened,
if comfort is to come to him and the waves of care grow cooler —
or else he must forever suffer agony
and grievous distress, so long as the handsomest of houses
stands towering on its summit."

Sitting on his stallion, the shore-watchman answered,
the doughty retainer: "A warlike shield-bearer
who judges wisely will surely know the difference
between words and deeds. From what I hear, this band
bears no malice

toward the prince of the Scyldings. Pass on, then,
with your weapons and armor. I will lead you myself;
and I will issue orders to my trusted vassals
to guard your excellent vessel from all harm —

your freshly tarred craft — against any opponent,
close by the seashore, until the curved-necked ship
shall bear the well-beloved hero back again
over the way of the water to the Weder lands.

To so great a warrior it shall surely be granted
to stand secure in the storm of strife."
Then they fared onward (the vessel lay quiet,
the broad-bosomed ship was bound fast by its cable,
firmly at anchor); the boar-figures glistened
bright on their visors, vivid with gilding,
flame-hardened and brilliant — the boar kept watch.
The heroes hastened, the warriors hurried,

and descended together, until they saw the great palace,
the well-fashioned feast-hall, wondrous and gleaming:

among the peoples and kindreds of the world, it was the most widely
known of halls under heaven — the hall in which the hero dwelt;
its radiance lit up countless lands.
Then the battle-brave warrior pointed out to them the glittering
court of the bold ones, so that they could easily
go onward on their journey. The aforementioned warrior,
turning his horse, spoke as he left them:

"It is time for me to be going. May the Father Almighty
grant you His grace, and give you safety on your journey
and on your mission! I will ride back to the sea
to stand as warden against hostile warriors."

chapters.title: Fitt VI — Beowulf Introduces Himself at the Palace
paragraphs:
The highway glistened with many-colored paving-stones,
and a path led the warriors along together.
Firm and hand-linked, the war-mail glistened;
the ringing sword rang bright among the armor
as the company approached the palace together

in their warlike gear. Against the wall of the building
they set down their broad war-shields, weary —
sturdy battle-shields. Then they turned toward the benches.
Their mail-coats rattled, the heroes' armor;
the lances stood upright, all in a cluster,
the seamen's weapons — ash-wood shafts
tipped with edges of iron. The armor-clad troop
was well-equipped with weapons.

Then a proud-minded hero questioned the champions
about their lineage: "From what borders
do you bring your plated war-shields, gilded and gleaming,
your gray mail-coats, helmets with visors,
and heap of war-lances? I am servant and retainer
to King Hrothgar. Never among folk from far lands
have I seen so many men of such courageous bearing.
I am sure it is out of valor — not as outlaws,
but out of greatness of soul — that you have sought King Hrothgar."

the friend-lord of the Danes, the giver of rings,
I will ask about your journey, as you urge me to do —
the famous folk-chief — and inform you promptly
of whatever answer the good one sees fit to give me."
He turned then hurriedly to where Hrothgar was sitting,
old and hoary, his earls attending him.
The strength-famed went until he stood at the shoulder
of the lord of the Danes — he minded the custom
of courteous thanes. Then Wulfgar addressed
his friendly liege-lord: "Men of the Geats

have been carried here over the way of the waters,
coming from far lands; the foremost in rank,
the battle-champions, call their leader Beowulf.
They make this petition: to be granted, O my chieftain,
a conference with you. O gracious King Hrothgar,
do not refuse to give them a friendly answer!

Judging by their war-gear, they seem worthy
of being honored among earls; surely the prince
who led these heroes hither is a doughty one."

chapters.title: Fitt VII — Hrothgar and Beowulf
paragraphs:
Hrothgar, protector of the Scyldings, answered:
"I remember this man as the merest of striplings.
His long-dead father was called Ecgtheow;
Hrethel the Geat gave him his only daughter at home.
His battle-brave son has now come here,
seeking a trustworthy friend.
Seafaring sailors asserted,

those who carried precious gift-treasures to the Geats
as peace-offerings, that this hero in battle
has the grip of thirty men in his hand.

The holy Creator has sent him to us,
I believe, to the West-Dane warriors,
to render gracious aid against Grendel's grimness.
I shall give the good one treasures for his courage.
Hasten to bid them come in quickly,
to see this assembled circle of kinsmen;
tell them plainly they are truly welcome
among the men of the Danes." To the door of the hall

Wulfgar went, and shouted out this word-message:
"My victorious liege-lord bade me tell you,
the prince of the East-Danes, that he knows your lineage,
and that you, valiant of spirit, borne here over the waves,
are welcome. You may enter straightaway
clad in your mail-coats, cased in your helmets,
to see King Hrothgar. Leave your battle-shields,
wood-spears, and war-shafts here to await your conference."
The mighty one rose then, with many a retainer,
an excellent troop of thanes; some remained behind
and, as the brave one ordered, guarded the battle-gear.
Together they hurried, while the hero guided them,
beneath Heorot's roof. The high-minded one walked on,
sturdy beneath his helmet, until he stood in the hall.
Beowulf spoke (his mail-coat glistened,
his armor seamed over by the craftsman's art):
"Hail to you, Hrothgar! I am Higelac's kinsman
and retainer; I have dared many a wonder
as a young man. The deeds of Grendel
I came to know fully in my far-off fatherland:
sea-farers tell us that this hall,
this excellent building, stands empty and useless
to all warriors once the evening-light's glimmer
beneath heaven's bright hues has hidden its glory.
Then my earls — the most excellent among them,
very clever men — urged me to come and assist you,
folk-leader Hrothgar; they knew well

the strength of my body. They had themselves seen me
when I came from battle, stained with gore,
having escaped from enemies — where I had bound five,
laid waste the race of giants, and destroyed
the sea-monsters by night in the waters.
I bore innumerable sorrows, avenged the Weders
(woes had they suffered), ravaged enemies.
And now, alone with Grendel,

I shall settle this matter, and with the evil monster,
the giant, decide it. So I would beg
this single petition of your bounty, chief of the Bright-Danes,
lord of the Scyldings, defender of warriors,
friend-lord of the people: do not refuse me —
since I have come so far to seek you —
that I alone, with my earls helping me,
this brave-minded war-band, may purify Heorot.
I have heard on inquiry that the horrible creature

in his utter recklessness cares nothing for weapons;
so I scorn them myself — may my beloved liege-lord Higelac
be gracious and lenient of spirit toward me —
and I shall carry neither blade nor broad-fashioned shield
into the onset. Only with my hand-grip

shall I grapple the foe and fight for my life,
foeman against foeman; he must rely on
the judgment of the Lord, whichever death lays hold of.
I am sure that, if he wins the struggle,
he will wish to eat the Geatish earls in the war-hall,
to swallow them boldly, as he has often done before
to the best of the Hrethmen! You will not need to trouble
about giving me a funeral; he will have me dripping
and dreary with gore, if death overtakes me —
he will bear me off bleeding, biting and mouthing me;
the solitary creature will eat me, heedless of pity,
and mark the moor-fens with blood. You will no longer need then

to find me my food. If I fall in battle,
send to Higelac the armor that shields my bosom,
the best of equipments, the richest of ring-mail;
it is the heirloom of Hrethel,
the work of Wayland. Fate goes ever as she must!"

chapters.title: Fitt VIII — Hrothgar and Beowulf — Continued
paragraphs:
Hrothgar, protector of the Scyldings, spoke:
"You have sought us here to defend our people
and offer your assistance, good friend Beowulf.

Your father engaged in the fiercest of feuds:
he killed Heatholaf in hand-to-hand combat
among the Wilfing warriors. Then the Weder people,
for fear of a feud, were forced to disown him,
and he fled from them to the folk of the South-Danes,
the race of the Scyldings, over the rolling waters.
I had only lately begun to govern the Danes;
I held in my youth the hoard-seat of heroes,
rich in its jewels. Heregar was dead,
my kinsman and elder had forsaken earth's joys —
Healfdene's son. He was a better man than I am!
I ended that feud afterward with a payment;
I sent old ornaments over the weltering waters
to the Wilfings, and your father swore oaths to me.

It pains me in spirit to tell anyone
what grief Grendel has caused me in Heorot,
what unlooked-for horror, through ceaseless hatred.
My war-band has waned, my hall-troop has wasted away;
Fate has cast them off into Grendel's clutches.
God can easily hinder the ravager
from such terrible deeds. Warriors in armor,
after drinking their beer, often promised
over the ale-cup that they would wait willingly
on the feasting benches for a grapple with Grendel,
with the grimmest of blade-edges.
Then in the morning this mead-hall was reeking with murder,
the building was bloody at daybreak,
the bench-planks all flooded, dripping and bloodied,
the folk-hall was gory. I had fewer retainers,
fewer dear warriors, whom death had laid hold of.

Sit down now at the feast, and show the heroes
your intentions and your victor-fame, as your spirit urges you!"
Then a bench in the cheerful beer-hall
was made ready for the men of the Geats gathered together;
warlike in spirit, they went to be seated,
proud and exultant. A retainer attended them,
bearing with decorum an ornamented goblet,
and poured out the gleaming drink. The minstrel sang

heartily in Heorot; there was rejoicing among the heroes,
a great gathering of Weders and Danes.

chapters.title: Fitt IX — Unferth Taunts Beowulf
paragraphs:
Unferth spoke up, the son of Ecglaf,
who sat at the feet of the lord of the Scyldings,
and opened the verbal sparring. Beowulf's journey,
the doughty sea-farer's, gave sorrow and bitter chagrin
to Unferth, for he never granted
that any other man on earth should attain
or gain under heaven more glory than himself:

"Are you the Beowulf who struggled with Breca,
who contended at swimming on the wide sea-currents,
where the two of you tried the ocean out of sheer pride,

and out of vainest boasting risked your bodies
in the grip of the waters? No one was able,
whether friend or foe, to dissuade you in the least
from your dangerous voyage. Then you ventured out swimming,
where with outstretched arms you covered the streams,
measured the sea-ways, mixing and stirring them,
and glided over the ocean. The waves were angry
with the turbulence of winter. In the water's grip
you toiled for seven nights; he outdid you at swimming,
excelled you in strength. Then early one morning
the sea-currents tossed him onto the shore of the Heathoremes,
and from there he sought the home of his fathers,
beloved of his people, the land of the Brondings,
the pleasant fortress, where he ruled a nation
and held stronghold and jewels. The pledge he made to you,

the son of Beanstan, he truly fulfilled.
So I expect you will have less fortunate results —

though you have always been triumphant in the onset of battle,
in grim grappling — if you dare await Grendel
close at hand for the space of a single night!"

Beowulf, the son of Ecgtheow, answered:
"My good friend Unferth, freely indeed and wildly,

fuddled with beer, you have spoken of Breca
and told of his journey! I claim as a fact
that I had greater strength in the waters then,
endured more hardship in the ocean, than any other man.
We made our agreement as the merest of striplings
and promised each other (we were both then

young in years) that we would venture out
upon the ocean; and we accomplished it all.
While swimming the sea-floods, we boldly brandished
unsheathed sword-blades; we expected to shield
our bodies from the sharks. He was certainly unable

to swim any further in the waters than I could,
nor move more swiftly on the waves — nor would I leave him.
Then the two of us companions stayed together in the ocean

for five nights, until the currents parted us,
the weltering waters, the bleakest weathers,
and the deepest night; and the north wind whistled
fiercely in our faces. The billows were terrible.
The sea-creatures' mood was mightily roused;
and there against enemies my firm-knotted mail-coat,
hand-linked and hardy, gave me help.
My braided battle-sark, brilliantly gilded,
lay on my bosom. A hateful fiend-ravager
dragged me to the bottom then, seized me and held me,
grim in his grip. Nevertheless it was granted me
to pierce the monster with the point of my weapon,
my obedient blade; the battle carried off
the mighty sea-creature by the strength of my hand.

chapters.title: Fitt X — Beowulf Silences Unferth — Glee is High
paragraphs:
"So ill-meaning enemies often caused me
the sorest sorrow. I served them in return,

with my beloved sword — as was fitting.
They missed out on the pleasure of feasting abundantly,
those evil-doers, missed eating my body,
surrounding the banquet deep in the ocean;
but wounded with sword-edges early in the morning,
they lay stretched out high on the strand of the ocean,

put to sleep by the sword, so that seafaring travelers
were no longer hindered after that from sailing
the foam-dashing currents. A light came from the east,
God's beautiful beacon; the billows subsided
so that I could clearly see the jutting headlands,

the blustering crags. Fate often saves
an undoomed hero if his valor is stout!
But it was my fortune to fell nine sea-monsters
with my weapon. I have rarely heard
of a harder night-struggle under the dome of heaven,
or of any creature more distressed in the waves of the ocean;
yet I escaped with my life from the grip of the monsters,

weary from the struggle. Then the waters bore me,
the flood with its current, to the land of the Finns,

the weltering waves. I have not heard a word told
of such daring deeds done by you, Unferth,
or of any sword-terror you inspired. Never has Breca,
at the play of battle, nor either of the two of you,
performed so fearless a feat with gleaming,
glinting weapons — I utter no empty boast;
though with cold-blooded cruelty you killed your brothers,
your nearest kin; and for that you must suffer
dire damnation in hell, however sharp your wits may be.
I tell you in earnest, son of Ecglaf,
Grendel, the dreadful demon, would never have done
such countless horrors to your liege-lord,
harrying in Heorot, if your heart were as sturdy,

your mood as ferocious, as you describe them.
He has discovered fully that the fierce-burning hatred,
the eager battle-edge, of all your kindred,
of the Victory-Scyldings, need little dismay him:
he takes his toll, he spares none

of the Danish people, but fights with pleasure,
kills and feasts — expecting no resistance

from the Spear-Danes. But the prowess and valor
of the Geatish earls shall soon venture
to give him a grapple. He who is able
shall go bravely to banquet, when the bright light of morning,

when the sun in its ether-robes which the second day brings
shines from the southward over the children of men!"
Then the gray-haired, war-famed giver of treasure

was blithe and joyous; the ruler of the Bright-Danes
expected aid; the protector of the people

had heard from Beowulf his bold resolve.
There was laughter among the heroes; loud was the clamor,
the words were pleasing. Then Wealhtheow came forward,

first to the lord of the kingdom, chief of the East-Danes,
and bade him be cheerful when the beer was flowing,
beloved by his retainers; he heartily tasted
the banquet and the beaker, the battle-famed ruler.
Then the Helmingish lady graciously moved
among all the retainers, lesser and greater,
offering treasure-cups, until the time came
that the dignified, diademed folk-queen

could bear the brimming cup to Beowulf.
She greeted the Geat-prince, and, most wise in her words,
thanked God that her wish had been accomplished,
that in some earl at last she could look for
solace in sorrow. The battle-bold warrior
accepted the beaker from Wealhtheow's hand,

then, equipped for combat, spoke in measured words.
Beowulf, the son of Ecgtheow, spoke:
"I resolved in spirit, when I embarked on the ocean,

when I boarded my boat with a band of my retainers,
that I would either work the will of your people
to the fullest, or fall in battle in the foe's clutches.
I shall perform deeds of daring and prowess,
or live the last of my days in this mead-hall."
These words — the boast of the Geat — were welcome and pleasing
to the lady; embroidered in gold trappings,
the freeborn folk-queen went to sit by her beloved lord.

Then once again, as before, courtly discussion
was heard in the building, the shouting of victors;
the heroes were happy, until the son of Healfdene
wished to go to his slumber to seek refreshment.
He knew that a fight with the horrid hell-monster
had been determined upon in the hall-building,
since they could no longer see the sun's light,
and lowering darkness had descended over all,
and dark under heaven shadowy shapes came gliding around them.

All the retainers rose then. One saluted the other —
Hrothgar saluted Beowulf — in formal verses,
wished him well, and, handing over the feast-hall
to his care and keeping, said as he departed:
"Never to anyone else have I entrusted,
but only to you, the hall of the Danes,
since first I could heave up my hand and my shield.
Take now in charge the noblest of houses;
be mindful of honor, display your prowess,
watch for the foe! You shall want for no enjoyments
if you survive so glorious an adventure!"

chapters.title: Fitt XI — All Sleep Save One
paragraphs:
Then Hrothgar departed, his troop of earls attending him,
the folk-lord of the Scyldings, out of the building;
the war-chieftain wished now to seek Wealhtheow,
the queen, as his bedmate. The Glory of Kings
had, as men recounted, given a hall-watch
to keep Grendel away: he performed a special service
for the king of the Danes, set a watcher against the giant.
And the prince of the Geats implicitly trusted

his warlike strength and the Lord's protection.
He took off his iron armor,
the helmet from his head, and handed to his attendant
his chased-hilted chain-sword, choicest of weapons,
and bade him guard his battle-equipment.
Then the good one spoke words of defiance,
Beowulf the Geat, before he mounted his bed:

"I hold myself no meaner in matters of prowess,
in warlike achievements, than Grendel himself;
so I shall not use a sword-edge to lull him to sleep
and take his life, though I well could do so.
He has no skill with weapons, to strike me blows
or shatter my shield, though he is surely mighty
in strife and destruction; but struggling by night
we shall do without weapon-edges, if he dare come
to weaponless warfare — and the wise-minded Father,
God ever-holy, shall assign the glory

and many an attending warrior of the sea-band
sank to his slumber. It seemed unlikely

that any of them should ever afterward hope
to be happy at home, visit hero-friends
or the lordly stronghold where he had lived from childhood.
They had heard how slaughter had recently seized
and carried off from the wine-hall far too many
of the race of the Scyldings.

But the Lord granted to them
the weaving of war-success — to the Weder heroes
He gave aid and comfort — so that they overcame
and vanquished every opponent through the war-might
of one man, through his own strength alone.
The truth is established, that God Almighty
has ruled for ages over kindreds and nations.
Through a very lurid night

the twilight traveler came tramping and striding.
The warriors who should have watched the horn-gabled building
were sleeping — all but one. It was known among men
that the implacable foe could not hurl them
to the land of shadows if the Lord was unwilling;
but Beowulf, serving as warder, a terror to foes,
angrily awaited the outcome of battle.

chapters.title: Fitt XII — Grendel and Beowulf
paragraphs:
Down from the cloud-dark cliffs came Grendel then,
striding from the moor, bearing God's anger.
The monster meant to trap one of the earthmen
in the grand hall and carry him off.
He moved beneath the sky until he came to
the wine-joyful building, gleaming with gold plate,
the gold-hall of warriors. This was not the first time

he had sought out Hrothgar's home and manor.
Never in the days of his life, before or after,
did he meet a harder hero, a hall-guard more steadfast.
Then the creature came striding toward the building,

cut off from joy. The door burst open at once,
though it was bound with forged iron bands, the moment his fingers touched it.
The fell one had flung it wide — his fury was so bitter —
the entrance stood open. A moment later
the enemy trod across the shining hall-floor,

striding in rage. From his eyes shone out
a hideous light, most like to flame.
He saw in the hall the warriors in their numbers,
a circle of kinsmen sleeping together,

a throng of warriors. His thoughts then leapt with triumph:
he meant to sever, before morning came,
the life from the body of every man there,
horrible demon, since fate had given him
the prospect of a feast. But Providence would not
let him devour any more of mankind
in the night. Hygelac's kinsman
was watching, pained to see how the savage creature
would carry out his sudden assault.
The monster had no thought of putting it off;

at the first chance he seized hold of
a soldier in his sleep, tore him apart at once,
bit through his bone-cage, drank the blood in streams,
swallowed him in great mouthfuls: soon he had eaten
the dead man's feet and hands completely.
Then he stepped closer — but the stout-hearted warrior

reached out for him as he lay still, gripping the enemy's hand;
the foeman lunged forward with his own outstretched arm,
and Beowulf caught that cunning schemer at once,
bracing himself on his elbow. The master of malice
knew in that instant that nowhere in middle-earth,
beneath the whole of the heavens, had he ever met

a hand-grip stronger than this in any man.
Fear seized his spirit, his courage began to fail,
but he could not break free; he was thinking of death,

longing to flee to his hiding place, to rejoin the devils' assembly:
his work now was not what it had been
through all the long years of his life. The worthy kinsman

of Hygelac now remembered his evening's boast,
stood up straight and took hold of him hard.
The monster's fingers cracked; the giant was straining outward,
the warrior pressed forward. The famous one meant
to flee farther off, if he could find any chance,
and away, without any delay,
to run to the fen-moors; he knew full well
that his strength in the grapple lay trapped in the foeman's grip.

It was an ill-starred journey that the harmful,
havoc-dealing raider had made to Heorot:

the palace rang and echoed; to all of the Danes,
to every dweller in the castle, to each of the bold men,
to the warriors, came terror. Both were furious,
the two hall-guardians raging. The building shook;
it was a marvelous wonder that the wine-hall held,
that it did not buckle to the ground
under their battle-fury — the splendid earth-hall;
but inside and out it had been bound so firmly
with iron bands, by the skill of the smith.
Off from its base, so men have told me,
many benches inlaid with gold-work were wrenched away,
where the grim two struggled. The wise Scyldings
had never before believed
that any man alive, by might and main-strength,
could shatter it apart, bone-decked, resplendent,
could break it by craft, unless the clutch of fire
should swallow it in smoke. A strange sound
rose up; terror fastened on the North Danes,
on every man who heard from the wall
the weeping and the lament,
the defeat-song of the enemy of heaven,
heard him howl his hymns of horror and bewail
his doom in hell. Beowulf held him too firmly —
he who was the strongest of all men in that age.

chapters.title: Fitt XIII — Grendel is Vanquished
paragraphs:
For nothing in the world would the warriors' defender
let that loathsome intruder keep his life-joys;
he judged the monster's existence to be utterly useless
to men under heaven. Many of Beowulf's noble companions
brandished their ancient battle-swords,
eager to guard the life of their lord and protector,
the far-famed chieftain, if only they could.
As they fought, the brave warriors did not know
that when they struck, meaning to carve the monster's body
into slivers and hunt down his spirit,
the relentless enemy could not be harmed by the finest blade
anywhere on earth, by any weapon of war:
he had sworn himself safe from victory-swords
and all such edged weapons. His death in that hour
was doomed to be wretched, and his exiled spirit
would travel far into the enemy's power.
Then he saw plainly, he who in his twisted joy
had worked such great malice for so long
against the race of men — an enemy of God —
that his body was giving way beneath him;
Hygelac's hardy thane and kinsman
held him by the hand. Each one was hateful

to the other while he lived. The fearful demon
suffered a body-wound — damage past healing
showed on his shoulder, his sinews split apart,
his body burst open. To Beowulf was given
glory in battle; Grendel now had to flee,
to hide himself in the fen-cliffs and marshes,
sick to death, to seek out his dwelling place,
joyless and woeful; he knew all the more clearly

that the end of his earthly life was near,
the limit of his days. For the Danes at last,
when the slaughter was over, their wish was fulfilled.
The stranger from afar had cleansed
the war-hall of Hrothgar from its evil,
wise and valiant, saved it from violence.
He took joy in the night's work, in his reputation for prowess;
the prince of the Geats had made good his boast
to the East-Danish people, had cured them fully
of the heavy sorrows, the malicious evil
they had suffered before, had endured
under crushing oppression — their long suffering.
It was a clear sign

when the battle-hero hung up the hand,
the arm and the shoulder — all of Grendel's claw together —
beneath the great vaulting hall-roof.

chapters.title: Fitt XIV — Rejoicing of the Danes
paragraphs:
In the morning mist, many a warrior
stood around the gift-hall, so the story goes:
chiefs of the people came from near and far
on long journeys to gaze at the wonder,
the footprints of the enemy. Few of the warriors

who looked on the tracks of that inglorious creature
felt much grief at his parting from life —
how, weary in spirit, beaten in combat,
he had dragged his trail away from those regions,
fated and fleeing, down to the water-monsters' pool.

There the currents bubbled with blood,
the angry eddies were stirred and churned,
seething with gore, welling up with sword-blood;
the death-doomed creature had hidden himself there,
stripped of all joy, and had laid down his life
in the lair to which he fled — his heathen spirit,
where hell received him. From there the old friends
turned back homeward, and many a young man
rode briskly from that glad adventure,
striding on stallions, returning from the sea,
heroes on horseback. Very often there could be heard

Beowulf's praises; many declared again and again
that no one, south or north, anywhere between the seas,

across the wide earth, under the arch of the sky,
was a better shield-bearing warrior,
none more worthy to rule.
Yet no one uttered any word of blame against
their own gracious friend and lord,

Hrothgar — he was a good king.
Now and again the famous riders let their fallow-coated horses
run in contest, racing and chasing,
wherever the country roads seemed fair and inviting,
known to be good; and now and then a thane of the king,

a man of reputation, skilled in verse,
who had ancient traditions stored in memory,
wove new phrases together in proper form:
the poet then began to tell of Beowulf's venture

with skill, to put clever words together
and speak them well, earnestly,
recounting everything he had heard about Sigmund's

mighty deeds — many things still little known,
the struggles of Wæls's son, the wide-ranging ventures
that the children of men knew only a little of,
his feuds and his fury. Only Fitela knew them,
when Sigmund chose to speak of such things,
uncle to nephew — for in every fight
each had always been devoted to the other:
together they had slain with the sword's edge
a great host of the race of enemies.
No small glory came to Sigmund
after his life-days were done,
since he, strong in struggle, had killed the great dragon,
guardian of the hoard. Under the gray stone
the prince's son ventured, alone,
on that perilous errand; Fitela was not with him.
Yet the luck fell to him of driving his weapon
through the marvellous dragon, so that the blade,
noble weapon, stood fast in the wall;
the worm lay slain.
The great one had earned by that glorious deed
the right to enjoy the ring-hoard to the fullest,
as most pleased him: he loaded his ship,
bore the shining treasures into the vessel's hold —
the kinsman of Wæls. The dragon melted in its own heat.

He was the most famous of wandering adventurers
among the far-flung peoples of the world, famous for great deeds,
shelter of warriors; and so his honor kept growing.

Afterwards, the hero-strength of Heremod failed him,
his vigor and his valor. Among venomous enemies
he was foully betrayed into the hands of foemen,
driven off early. Waves of torment

oppressed him too long, until he became to his people,
to all the nobles, an unbearable burden;
and in years past many wise men
had often lamented the daring one's turning,
such as had hoped he would bring them help in their sorrow —
that the son of their ruler would rise into power,
taking up the leadership his fathers had held,
that he would govern the people, the gold-hoard, the city,
the kingdom of heroes, the realm of the Scyldings.

But now Hygelac's kinsman Beowulf became
far more beloved to all men, to kindreds and races,
and dearer to his friends; malice had assaulted Heremod.
Time and again the riders measured out the fallow highways,
racing their horses along them. Then the light of morning
quickened and hurried on. Many thanes,
bold in spirit, went to the beautiful building
to gaze at the wonder; and the king himself,
keeper of treasures, came out from his queen's chamber
with a great glorious retinue, famous for his virtues,
and with him the queen walked the mead-paths,
her maidens attending her.

chapters.title: Fitt XV — Hrothgar's Gratitude
paragraphs:
Hrothgar spoke — he went up to the hall,
stood at the pillar, saw the steep-rising hall-roof
gleaming with gold, and Grendel's hand there:

"For the sight we behold now, let thanks be given
at once to the Ruler! Much evil I have borne,
grief at Grendel's hands; God can always work
wonder upon wonder, Lord of Glory!

Just lately I thought I would never, under heaven,
find comfort for any of my sorrows,
while the handsomest of houses stood towering,
stained and horrible with blood; grief had shaken
each of my wise counselors, who did not believe they could ever
strengthen the people's defenses against enemies,
against spirits and monsters. Now, through the might of the Ruler,
a single brave warrior has accomplished a deed
that before this all of us, with all our excellent wisdom,

had failed to do. Truly one may say,
whatever woman among the nations
gave birth to this child — if she is still alive —
that the eternal Lord was generous to her
in the bearing of that son. Now, dear Beowulf,

best of heroes, I will love you in my heart
as my own son; keep well from now on
this new kinship. You shall never lack
any of the earth-joys I can give you.
Often for lesser service I have given
treasure to a less hardy hero,

to a weaker man in war. By deeds of distinction
you have now gained for yourself that your glory will flourish
forever and ever. May the All-Ruler reward you
with good from His hand, as He has done until now!"

Beowulf spoke in answer, Ecgtheow's son:
"That labor of glory we achieved gladly,
we finished the fight, unshrinking we faced
the enemy's grasp. I would have liked it far more
if you could have seen the creature in person,
sinking, failing, the foe in his gear!
I meant to bind him fast on his death-bed at once
with firm-holding fetters, so that under my grip
he would have lain low in a life-and-death struggle
unless his body could slip away. I could not hold him back,

not that this gave the wretched creature any comfort:
the hated destroyer
lives no longer, scourged for his evils —
sorrow has taken hold of him, has trapped him
in its snares, keeps him writhing
in cruel bonds; there, banished for his wickedness,
the creature must wait for the great judgment,

for what the God of glory will give him as his wages."
Then the warrior grew silent, the son of old Ecglaf,

from boasting and bragging of his own battle-deeds,
since the princes saw, hanging beneath the lofty hall-timbers
by the might of that nobleman,
the enemy's fingers laid out before each of them;
each fingernail looked most like hardened steel,
the heathen's hand-spur, the battle-warrior's
uncanny claw. They agreed as one

that no fine edge of any brave man's sword
would have touched him — no blade could ever have cut away
that terrible creature's bloody battle-hand.

chapters.title: Fitt XVI — Hrothgar Lavishes Gifts Upon His Deliverer
paragraphs:
Then the order went out at once that Heorot inside
be set right by hand: a host of men and women
gathered and prepared the guest-hall, the feast-building.
Gold-embroidered tapestries shone out along the walls,
full of wonders for every hero
who looked upon such things.

The beautiful building had been broken to pieces
even though every part of it had been bound with iron;
its hinges had been torn away. Only the roof
was still whole and uninjured when the terrible creature,
outlawed for his evils, had crept away,
despairing of his life. It is hard to escape
the end, whoever will attempt it;

everyone must come in time to the place
that has been appointed — as fate has set down
for all soul-bearers, earth-dwellers, nobles under heaven —
where their body shall lie bound to its bed

when feasting is done. The time had now come
for the son of Healfdene to enter the hall;
the great prince meant to take part in the banquet.
I have never heard of a people with a larger company
comporting themselves better toward their ring-giver.
The glory-laden men bowed to the benches
(their kinsmen and companions were full of joy,
draining many a cup with pleasure),
bold in spirit in the high-towering palace,

Hrothgar and Hrothulf. Heorot was now filled within
with friends; the Folk-Scyldings
were not yet practicing any falsehood or treachery.

Then the son of Healfdene presented to Beowulf
a golden standard as reward for the victory,
an embroidered banner, mail-coat, and helmet;
many men saw a famous sword
borne before the hero. Beowulf drank
from the cup in the hall; that gift of treasure
he had no reason to be ashamed of in the presence of warriors.

I have never heard of many men at an ale-bench
presenting four bright jewels adorned with gold-work
to their fellows in friendlier fashion.
Around the crown of the helmet, a ridge-piece
braided with wire and studded with bosses
ran along the outside as a head-guard,
so that battle-hardened swords could not harm him
when the hero set out

against his enemies. Then the protector of nobles
ordered that eight horses with gold-plated,
gleaming bridles be led into the hall;
on one of them stood a saddle richly worked
with art and set with jewels — it was the king's own seat,
where the son of King Healfdene sat when he took part
in the play of the sword-edges;
the famous one's valor never failed at the front
when the slain were falling. And to Beowulf the lord
of the Ingwins granted power over both,
over the war-horses and the weapons, and bade him
enjoy them well. In so manly a way
the mighty-famed chieftain, hoard-keeper of heroes,
repaid the storms of battle with horses and jewels
that no one who is willing to tell the truth in full fairness
will ever condemn him.

chapters.title: Fitt XVII — Banquet (continued) — The Scop's Song of Finn and Hnæf
paragraphs:
And the prince of warriors gave to each of the heroes
who had crossed the sea-roads with Beowulf
a costly gift at the mead-bench,
presented an heirloom, and ordered that compensation in gold
be paid for the man whom Grendel had earlier
wickedly slaughtered — and he would have killed more of them
had not far-seeing God and the courage of the hero
turned fate aside. The Father was governing
all earth-dwellers then, as He does always;
that is why insight is most fitting everywhere for all men,
foresight of spirit. Much both of good and of evil
will a man have to bear who long in this present world
uses his life in this woeful existence.
There was music and merriment mingled together
in honor of Healfdene's leader; the harp was played,
verses recited, when the bard of Hrothgar
at the mead-bench came to speak of the merry hall-joy
of the kinsmen of Finn, when assault surprised them:

"The half-Danish hero Hnæf of the Scyldings
was fated to perish on the field of the Frisians.
Hildeburg had no reason to praise
the faith of the Jutes. Blameless though she was,

when shields were splintered she was cut off from her loved ones,
from sons and brothers: they went down to their fate
wounded by the war-spear; woeful was that woman.
Not without cause did Hoce's daughter lament
the decree of the Ruler when morning light came
and she was able, under heaven, to behold the slaughter
of her brothers and sons, there where the brightest of earth-joys
had been hers until then. War had swept off
all of Finn's warriors, except for a small handful,
so that he could not in any way offer resistance

to Hengest's onset on the field of battle,
nor rescue the wretched remnant from war
against the prince's earl; so they offered terms:

another great building would be fully made ready,
a hall with a high-seat, which the Danes might share rule of
together with the sons of the Jutes, and that Folcwalda's son
would day after day honor the Danes
at the giving of gifts, and would share of his ring-store
with Hengest's men just as freely,
of his gold-plated treasures, even as he cheered the Frisians

at the bench of the beer-hall. On both sides they then swore
a binding compact; Finn solemnly vowed to Hengest,
with no thought of revoking it,
that he would properly take charge of the woe-stricken remnant,
as his counselors advised him; and that no one
should ever weaken the agreement by words or deeds,
should shatter it or injure its worth by any trick,
even though, robbed of their ruler, the Danes now had to follow
their own ring-giver's slayer as his retainers, since fate demanded it.

Should any of the Frisians speak of the old quarrel
in taunting tones, the terrible sword-edges
should cut him down in return. The oath was sworn,
and treasure of gold was lifted up from the hoard.

The best of the Scylding warriors was then fully
made ready for the pyre; at the pile one could see plainly
the blood-stained mail-coat, the boar-crest with its gilding,
the iron-hard swine, and many nobles
with fatal wounds; not a few had been slaughtered.
Hildeburg then ordered, at the burning of Hnæf,

that the son of her own body be carried to the fire,
that his body be burned and borne to the pyre.
The woe-stricken woman wept on his shoulder,
sang her lament; the hero rose up into the flames.
The greatest of funeral-fires curled toward the sky,
crackled on the hilltop; heads were melting,
wound-gashes bursting, as blood gushed out
from the fierce body-bite. The fire devoured them,
greediest of spirits, whom war had carried off
from both peoples; their bravest had fallen.

chapters.title: Fitt XVIII — The Finn Episode (continued) — The Banquet Continues
paragraphs:
"Then the warriors departed to go back to their homes,
stripped of their friends, to see Friesland again,
their homes and their stronghold. Hengest stayed on,

living with Finn through the blood-tainted winter,
never leaving him; yet he thought of his fatherland,
though he could not drive his ring-prowed ship
over the ocean paths — the sea-deeps were heaving,
fighting against the wind; winter locked the currents
in ice-bonds, until in its course there came to the land
another year, as it still turns now,
the world-cheering weathers one always looks for
when the season is fair. Then winter was past,
the earth's bosom was lovely; the exile longed to leave,

the guest in the palace; but he brooded on grim revenge
more eagerly than on any sea-voyage,
wondering whether he could bring about an attack
that would call the sons of the Jutes to account.
He did not refuse the duty of a retainer
when Hun of the Frisians placed the battle-sword Láfing,
fairest of blades, into his hand as a friendly gift:
its edges were famous in the folk-talk of Jutland.
And in turn a savage sword-fury seized
bold-spirited Finn where he sat in his palace,

when Guthlaf and Oslaf mournfully spoke
of the grim grappling, after their sea-journey,
and laid part of the blame on him; the restless spirit
could not be kept in his chest. Then the hall was covered

with the corpses of enemies, and Finn too was slain,
the king with his companions, and the queen taken captive.
The Scylding troops carried down to their ships
everything the land-king had kept in his palace,
such trinkets and treasures as they could find
when they searched Finn's home. They ferried to Daneland
that noble woman on the sea-journey,
led her back to her own people." The lay was ended,
the minstrel's recital. Cheers rose again,
bench-glee resounded, the cup-bearers poured

wine from wondrous vessels. Then Wealhtheow came forward,
walking beneath her golden crown, to where the two good ones were seated,
uncle and nephew; their peace was still mutual,
each true to the other. And Unferth the spokesman
sat at the feet of the lord of the Scyldings:
each trusted that the other's heart was brave,
though he had failed his kinsmen in faith during a fight.
Then the queen of the Scyldings spoke: "My lord and protector,
treasure-giver, take this cup;
may joy be with you, gold-friend of warriors,

and greet the Geats with gracious words!
That is how one should act. Be kind to the Geats,
not stingy with gifts; both near and far
you now enjoy peace. I have been told
that you mean to take the battle-brave hero as a son.
Heorot is cleansed now, the ring-palace gleaming;

give out many rewards while you still may,
and leave the kingdom and the people to your own kin
when you go on your way to the Ruler's splendor.
I know good Hrothulf — that he will care for
and honor the young warriors,

lord of the Scyldings, if you finish your earth-joys
before he does; I trust that he will repay our sons
with kindness, and our descendants too,
if he remembers all the favors we gave him in the past,
when he was still an infant,
for his comfort and his pleasure."
Then she turned to the bench where her sons were feasting,
Hrethric and Hrothmund, and the sons of the heroes,

the war-youth together; there the good one was sitting
between the two brothers — Beowulf the Geat.

chapters.title: Fitt XIX — Beowulf Receives Further Honor
paragraphs:
A cup was brought to him, and an invitation to drink
graciously given, and twisted gold
presented with pleasure — a pair of arm-jewels,
rings and a mail-shirt, the greatest of neck-rings
I have heard of beneath heaven. Of no hero
under the sky have I heard greater treasures given,

since Hama carried off the Brosings' necklace,
the jewels and brooches, from the bright-shining city,
fleeing Eormenric's cunning treachery,
choosing lasting reward. Hygelac of the Geats,
grandson of Swerting, last held this jewel
when he marched beneath his banner guarding the treasure,
defending the spoils of the field; fate carried him off
when he endured calamity on account of his daring,
the hatred of the Frisians. He had worn those ornaments
across the cup of the currents, those costly gem-treasures,
the mighty leader of the people; he fell beneath his shield.
The corpse of the king then came into the possession
of the Franks, the mail-coat and the collar:
warriors of lesser worth plundered the fallen
after the fight was finished. The Geats
were left holding the field of the slain.
The finest of mead-halls rang with cheering.
Wealhtheow spoke, addressing the company:
"Enjoy this collar in safety, worthy Beowulf,
young man, and make good use of this armor,
treasures of the people, and prosper well,
show yourself strong, and be to these warriors
gentle with your counsel! I will not forget your reward.
You have brought it about that far and near,
forever and ever, men shall honor you,
as widely as the ocean surrounds
the windy headlands. Be, as long as you live,
a prosperous prince. I wish you truly
jewels and treasure. Be kind to my son,
living in joy! Here each of the nobles
is true to every other, gentle in spirit,
loyal to the leader. The retainers are peaceful,
the warriors ready; well-drunken heroes,
do as I bid you." Then she went to her seat.
There was the finest of banquets; the heroes drank wine:

they did not know their fate, the cruel destiny
that had already befallen many of them,
as it happens to many a noble.
When evening had come and Hrothgar had gone off
to his own quarters, the mighty one going to his rest,
warriors beyond counting guarded the building,
as they had often done before. They cleared the ale-benches;
the whole floor was covered over with beds and pillows.

Doomed to his death, one of the beer-thanes
bowed down to his sleep. They set their battle-shields,
their bright-gleaming bucklers, at the heads of their beds;
above each noble on his bench it was easy to see
his lofty battle-helmet, his ring-mail coat,

and his mighty war-spear. It was the custom of that people
to keep themselves always ready for battle,
whether at home or on the march — in either condition —
at any moment when the need might come
to serve their lord; they were a worthy people.

chapters.title: Fitt XX — The Mother of Grendel
paragraphs:
They sank down to sleep. One of them paid with sorrow
for his evening rest, as had often happened to them
while Grendel held the gold-adorned palace,
working evil, until his end came upon him,
death for his sins. It was very clearly seen,

widely known among men, that an avenger
still outlived the hated creature, long after the grief
caused by that struggle. The mother of Grendel,
a monstrous woman, kept her own sorrow in mind;
she was said to live in the horrible waters,

the cold-running currents, ever since Cain had become
a slayer by the sword of his one and only brother,
his father's son. He went out then, banished,
marked as a murderer, shunning the joys of men,
and lived in the wilderness. From him many demons

awoke, sent forth by fate; one of them was Grendel,
the sword-cursed, hateful one, who at Heorot came upon
a man keeping watch, waiting for the fight,
where that horrible one gripped him in a mighty hand-grapple;
but the man remembered the strength of his body,
the glorious gift God had given him,
and trusted in the favor of the people-ruling Father,
His help and His comfort — and so conquered the enemy,
humbled the hell-spirit, who departed from there wretched,
stripped of his joy, setting out for the haunts of death,
enemy of mankind. But his mother,

eager and grim, was bent on making her own
mournful journey, mindful of vengeance
for the death of her son. She came then to Heorot
where the Armor-Danes lay all through the building,
sleeping. A sudden change came upon the nobles
when the mother of Grendel
entered the hall. The terror was less severe
only by as much as the strength of a maiden,
the war-strength of a woman, is less than a warrior's,
when a well-carved weapon, shaped by the hammer,
its blade very bloody, bold with its edges,
crashes down on the boar-crest that stands on the helmet.
Then hard-edged weapons were snatched up all through the building,
blades lifted over the benches, many a broad linden-shield
held fast in the hand; no one thought of helmet
or broad mail-coat when terror took hold of him.
She then went quickly, meaning to get out
to save her life once she was spotted;
but she had soon laid hold of one of the nobles
fast and firmly, and hurried off toward the fens.
He was the dearest of heroes to Hrothgar,
of all his retainers between the encircling seas,
a mighty shield-warrior, whom she murdered at his sleep,
a widely-famed battle-knight. Beowulf was not present there,

for another chamber had earlier been given
to the glory-decked Geat, after the distribution of gold.
There was uproar in Heorot. She had snatched
the famous hand, still gory, in her grip; grief was renewed
in homes and houses: it was no happy exchange
that both sides had to buy and pay for
with the lives of their friends. Then the old ruler,
the gray-haired war-thane, was stricken in spirit
when he knew that his long-trusted retainer was dead,
his dearest one gone. Swiftly Beowulf was summoned
from his chamber, brave and triumphant.
As day was dawning in the dusk of morning,

the noble warrior, the champion, went with his companions
to where the wise king was waiting
to see whether all-gracious God would grant him any relief
after the grief he had suffered. The battle-worthy hero
with his band of retainers trod across the pavement
(the hall-floor thundered under them), until he greeted the wise king,

the lord of the Ingwins; he asked whether the night had
been fully refreshing to him, as he had hoped.

chapters.title: Fitt XXI — Hrothgar's Account of the Monsters
paragraphs:
Hrothgar answered, protector of the Scyldings:
"Do not ask about joy! Grief is renewed again
for the Danish people. Æschere is dead,
elder brother of Yrmenlaf,
my true-hearted counsellor, my trusted adviser,
my shoulder-companion, the one who guarded my head
when we fought in battle and the troops clashed,

when the warriors struck; such a man should a noble ever be,
a truly worthy prince, as Æschere proved himself to be.
In Heorot the restless death-spirit
became his hand-to-hand murderer; I cannot say where
the cruel one, exulting in the carcass,

went off gorged with her prey. She took that revenge
for the killing you did last night — when you slew Grendel
in the most terrible fashion, with a grim-holding grip,
since he had for too long thinned my household
and wasted my people so foully. He fell in the fight,
forfeiting his life, and now another has come in his place,
a mighty doer of crimes, avenging her kinsman,
and from now on she has made her hatred unyielding,
as may well seem plain to many a retainer
who mourns in spirit the treasure-giver,
the heavy heart-sorrow; the hand lies lifeless now
that used to grant you every wish you cherished.
I have heard people of this land, my retainers,
dwellers in the halls, saying they have very often seen
a pair of such great march-striding creatures,
far-dwelling spirits, haunting the moorlands:
one of them wore, as they could well see,
the shape of a woman; the other, wretched,
in the form of a man walked the paths of exile,
except that he was bigger than any other man;
earth-dwelling people in the old days called him Grendel;
they do not know his father, whether any other evil spirits
were ever born to him

before. They guard the wolf-coverts,
lands no one can reach, wind-beaten headlands,
the most dreadful fen-deeps, where a flood from the mountains
rattles downward beneath mists on the cliffs,
the stream running under the earth. It is not far from here,
measured in miles, that the mere-water stands,
over which forests hang, frost-whitened,
a firm-rooted forest, the waters overshadowed.
There every night an ominous wonder may be seen,
fire on the water; not one of the children of men
lives wise enough to know its bottom.
Though the heath-stepper, harassed by hounds, may make for it,

the firm-antlered stag, fleeing into the forest,
driven from far off — he will give up his life,
sooner yield his spirit on the bank than venture in
to hide his head there. It is an uncanny place;
from there the surging of waters rises upward,
dark against the sky, when the wind stirs up
the ugly weathers, until the air grows gloomy
and the heavens darken. Now help must come
from you, and from you only! You do not yet know the place,
the dangerous spot where you may meet with
that sin-laden creature: seek it, if you dare!
I will pay you fully for this feud with money,
with ancient treasure, as I did before,
with well-twisted jewels, if you come back alive."

chapters.title: Fitt XXII — Beowulf Seeks Grendel's Mother
paragraphs: Beowulf spoke in answer, Ecgtheow's son:

"Do not grieve, wise king! For every man
it is better to avenge his friend than to mourn him too long;
each of us must await the end-day
of his earthly life; let the man who can
gain glory before death! For a noble warrior
who lies dead, that is in the end what fits best.
Rise up, king, let us hurry at once
to look at the trail of Grendel's kinswoman!
I promise you this now: she shall not escape to her place,
not into the earth's embrace, not into any mountain forest,
nor into the depths of the sea, wherever she tries to go.
For today endure each of your sorrows
with patience, as I truly expect of you!"
Then the old king sprang up, giving thanks to the All-Ruler,
Almighty Lord, that the man had spoken so.
Then for Hrothgar a war-horse was fitted with bridle,
a curly-maned courser. The wise people-leader

set out in state; a troop of shield-bearers
stepped out behind him. Her footprints could be seen
plainly along the wood-paths, her way across the ground
as she had gone far off over the murky fen-country,
carrying with her, lifeless, the best of the retainers
who had pondered with Hrothgar over the welfare of the land.
Then the prince passed over
the stony, steeply dropping cliffs, the close-covered paths,
the narrow passes, unfrequented tracks,
abrupt headlands, many haunts of water-monsters;
one of only a few wise-minded heroes,
he went on ahead to scout the surroundings,
until all at once he found mountain-woods
hanging over gray stones, a joyless forest;
the water stood below, welling up and gory.
It was painful in spirit to all of the Danes,
the friends of the Scyldings, to many a retainer,

hard to bear, a sorrow not small
to each of the warriors, when they came upon Æschere's head
on the cliff. The current was seething
with blood and with gore (the soldiers gazed at it).
Soon the horn sang the battle-song, ready for war.
The troop sat down; along the water they saw

many a serpent, wondrous sea-dragons
trying the waters, water-monsters lying
on the cliffs of the headlands — creatures that at midday often
set out on the sea-deeps on their sorrowful journeys,
wild beasts and serpent-kind; they hurried off then

hot-tempered, hateful, when they heard the great clamor,
the war-trumpet winding. One of them the prince of the Geats
cut off from earth's joys with an arrow from his bowstring,
tore him from his sea-struggle, so that the trusty war-shaft

pierced him to the vitals; he proved in the currents
less strong at swimming now that death had taken him.
Soon in the waters the wondrous swimmer
was hard pressed with sword-pointed boar-spears,
taken by force, and dragged up onto the cliff-edge;
the retainers looked upon the loathsome stranger.

Beowulf then put on his battle-gear,
caring little for his life. His inlaid, ample,
hand-woven mail-coat, which could cover his body,
was now to search the wave-deeps, so that war could not
harm the great hero, and the hater's grip
could not endanger his safety. His head was protected
by the bright-shining helmet that was to plunge into the deeps,
to brave the eddies — a helmet emblazoned with treasure,
ringed with jewels, just as in seasons long ago
the weapon-smith had worked it, making it wondrously,
fashioning it with swine-crests, so that from that day on
no blade could bite it, no battle-sword could hurt it.
And another thing of no small help in his prowess
was what Hrothgar's spokesman had lent him in his need;
the hilted hand-sword was called Hrunting,
old and most excellent among all the treasures;
its blade was of iron, stained with poison,
hardened with battle-gore; it had never failed in battle
any hero under heaven who held it in his hand,
who dared to take the terrible journeys,
who sought out the battle-field; this was not the first time
it had been destined to accomplish deeds of daring.

Ecglaf's kinsman clearly did not now remember,
proud in his own strength, what he had said before,
drunken with wine, when he lent that weapon
to a bolder swordsman. He himself did not dare
to risk his life beneath the surging of the currents,
to do deeds of fame; there he forfeited glory,
his reputation for strength. Not so with the other one,
when he had clad himself in his mail-coat, ready for battle.

chapters.title: Fitt XXIII — Beowulf's Fight with Grendel's Mother
paragraphs:
Beowulf spoke, son of Ecgtheow:
"Remember now, famous kinsman of Healfdene,
most prudent prince, now that I am ready to depart,
gold-friend of warriors, what we agreed upon before:
if I should lay down my life in helping you,
when my earthly joys were ended, you would always act
as a father to me; protect and care for
my faithful thanes, my trusty retainers,
if I fall in battle. And, beloved Hrothgar,
send to Higelac the precious jewels
you have given me. The lord of the Geats,
the son of Hrethel, may see from the gold,

when he looks on the treasures, that I found a gem-giver
excellent beyond measure, and enjoyed his friendship while I could.
And let Unferth have the ancient heirloom,
the famed man — the splendid heavy-sword,
the hard-edged weapon. With Hrunting to aid me,
I shall win glory, or grim death shall take me."

The prince of the Geats spoke these words and
hurried forth heroically, unwilling to wait
for any reply. The wave-current swallowed

the warrior bold in battle. Then a full day passed before
he could see the sea's bottom.
She soon discovered — she who for fifty winters
had held the course of the currents in her fury,
grisly and greedy — that one of the men from above
was exploring the grim one's dominion.

She reached out and grabbed him, gripped the warrior
with her horrible claws; yet she could not harm
his unscathed body: the mail-coat guarded him well,
so that she could not pierce through the armor,
the locked limb-mail, with her loathsome-grasping fingers.
The sea-wolf then, when she reached the bottom,
bore the ring-prince homeward, so that he could not —

though he had the courage for it —
wield his weapons against her,
and many a sea-beast tormented him as he swam,

no few flood-beasts with fierce-biting tusks
broke at his mail-coat, pursuing the brave one.
The earl then discovered he was down in some cavern
where no water in any way harmed him,
and the clutch of the current could not come near him,
since the roofed hall prevented it. He saw a brightness,
a firelight, gleaming resplendent.
Then the good man saw the sea-bottom's monster,
the mighty mere-woman. He made a great onset
with his battle-weapon; his hand did not hold back
from striking, so that the war-blade struck her head
with a greedy battle-song. The stranger then saw

that the sword would not bite, would not harm her life —
the falchion failed the folk-prince in his need.
Before it had often met onsets,
often cloven the helmet, the doomed man's armor:
it was the first time ever that the excellent jewel
had failed of its fame. Firm-minded afterwards,
not careless of valor, but mindful of glory,
was Higelac's kinsman. The angry hero-chief
threw aside his carved sword, adorned with jewels,
so that it lay on the ground, hard and steel-pointed.

He trusted in his strength, his sturdy hand-grip.
So must any man act whenever he means
to win in battle unending glory,
and is reckless of his life. The lord of the War-Geats
(he did not shrink from the fight) seized by the shoulder
Grendel's mother. Then, mighty in struggle,
he swung his enemy, since his anger was kindled,
so that she fell to the floor. With a furious grip

she gave him requital soon afterwards,
and reached out to grab him. The strongest of warriors,
faint-hearted, stumbled until he fell in his tracks,
the foot-fighter champion. Then she sat on her hall-guest
and drew her war-knife, wide-bladed and flashing,
to take vengeance for her son, her one only child.

The woven breast-armor lay on his shoulder;
it guarded his life, held off the entrance
of sword-point and edges. Ecgtheow's son there
would have perished fatally, champion of the Geats,
in the arms of the ocean, had not the armor given,
the close-woven corslet, comfort and help,

and had not holy God awarded the victory,
the all-knowing Lord. Easily did heaven's
most righteous Ruler decide it with justice;
the hero rose up, ready once more for battle.

chapters.title: Fitt XXIV — Beowulf is Double-conqueror
paragraphs:
Then among the war-treasures he saw a weapon of victory,
an ancient giant-sword with mighty edges,
the glory of warriors: it was the choicest of weapons,
except that it was larger than any other man
would have been able to bear to battle —
the splendid handiwork of the giants.
He grasped the sword-hilt then, the Scylding knight,
bold and battle-grim, brandished the ringed sword,
hopeless of his life, and struck her fiercely,
so that the blade gripped hard at the fiend-woman's neck,

broke through her bone-joints; the bill pierced fully
her fate-cursed body, and she fell to the ground.
The hand-sword was bloody; the hero exulted.
The blade shone brilliant, glimmered brightly,
just as the torch of the firmament shines gemlike
from heaven. He looked along the hall,
and turned by the wall. Higelac's vassal,
raging and wrathful, raised his battle-sword
strong by the handle. The edge was not useless
to the hero in battle, for he quickly wished
to give Grendel payment for the many assaults
he had worked on the West-Danes, not once but often,
when he slew Hrothgar's men in their sleep,
devoured fifteen sleeping retainers
of the Danish people, and carried away
just as many — a horrible prey.
He gave him his requital, the grim-raging champion,

when he saw on his resting-place, weary of conflict,
Grendel lying, bereaved of life's joys,
as the battle at Heorot had earlier scathed him.
His body bounded far when he suffered the blow —
death having seized him — a heavy sword-stroke,
and then Beowulf cut off his head. Soon this was noticed
by the clever men who, as Hrothgar's comrades,
gazed on the sea-deeps: the surging wave-currents
were mightily troubled, the mere was gory.
The gray-haired men talked together about the good warrior,

the hoary-headed, saying they no longer hoped to see
the prince again, that he would return rejoicing in victory
to visit the distinguished folk-ruler.
Many concluded that the mere-wolf had killed him.
The ninth hour came. Then the bold-minded Scyldings
departed from the headland; the gold-friend of heroes
took himself home. The strangers sat down,
soul-sick and sorrowful, watching the sea-waves;
they wished, yet did not expect, to see
their well-loved friend-lord

anymore. Then the sword-blade,
the blood having touched it, began to shrivel
with battle-icicles. It was a wonderful marvel
that it melted entirely, much like ice when
the Father unbinds the bond of the frost
and unwinds the wave-bands — He who wields dominion
over times and tides, a true-firm Creator.
Nor did he take more of the jewels from the dwelling,
the lord of the Weders, though they lay all around him,
than the head, and the handle handsome with jewels.
The blade had melted early, the weapon was burnt:
so hot was the blood, the poisonous strange-spirit

that had perished in it. He soon swam away then,
he who had endured the carnage of haters in combat,
and went up through the ocean. The eddies were cleansed,
the spacious expanses, when the alien spirit
laid aside his life and this short-lived existence.
The seamen's defender came swimming to land then,
doughty in spirit, rejoicing in his sea-gift,
the bulky burden which he carried in his keeping.
The excellent vassals advanced to meet him,
grateful to God, glad in their chieftain,
that it was granted them to see him safe and sound.
From the high-minded hero, then, helmet and mail-coat
were quickly loosened. The ocean was foul,
the water beneath the sky churned with gore.
They set out then, retracing their footsteps,
merry and glad, measured the earth-road,
the familiar highway: very daring men.
Then they bore the head from the sea-cliff, burdening
each of the earls, excellent and valiant.

Four of them had to carry with labor
the head of Grendel to the high-towering gold-hall,
stuck up on the spear, until fourteen most-valiant
and battle-brave Geats came walking there
straight to the palace: the prince of the people
strode the mead-ways, their brave-hearted companion.
The prince of earls entered the building,
the deed-valiant man, adorned with distinction,
the doughty shield-warrior, to address King Hrothgar:
then hung by its hair, the head of Grendel
was borne into the hall where the beer-thanes were drinking,
loathsome before the earls and before the lady too:
the warriors beheld then a wonderful sight.

chapters.title: Fitt XXV — Beowulf Brings His Trophies — Hrothgar's Gratitude
paragraphs:
Beowulf spoke, son of Ecgtheow:
"Look! we have gladly brought you, son of Healfdene,
prince of the Scyldings, these gifts from the ocean
which your eye beholds, as an emblem of glory.
I came away from this alive, narrowly escaping:
in the war beneath the water I performed the work
with great pains, and the fight had very nearly ended
had God not defended me. With Hrunting's help
I could not accomplish anything in the battle,
though that weapon was worthy; but the Ruler of men

willingly allowed me to see on the wall
a heavy old hand-sword hanging in splendor
(He most often guides the lost and the friendless),
