and I swung it as a weapon. In the conflict then
I killed the wards of the house (when the chance was given me).
Then the battle-sword burned, the blade that was lifted,
as the blood-current sprang, hottest of war-sweats;
seizing the hilt, I carried it off from my foes;
I avenged, as I ought, their acts of malice,
the murder of the Danes. I now make you this promise:

you will be able to sleep without care in Heorot
with your throng of heroes and the thanes of your people,
each and every one, both greater and lesser;
and you need not fear for them from that same direction
as you formerly feared, O folk-lord of the Scyldings,
an end-day for your warriors." To the aged man then,

the gray-haired chieftain, the gold-fashioned sword-hilt,
the old work of giants, was then given;
since the fall of the fiends, it passed into the keeping
of the lord of the Danes, the wonder-smith's labor;
and when the evil-minded being abandoned this world,
the opponent of God, victim of murder,
and his mother too, it went into the keeping
of the best of the world-kings between the encircling seas,
who dealt out treasure in the Scylding realm.

Hrothgar spoke, and studied the hilt,
the ancient heirloom where the beginning of an old-time
conflict was engraved: the gurgling currents,
the flood afterward slew the race of the giants —
they had acted proudly; that people was hostile to

the everlasting Lord, and through the lash of the billows
the Father gave them their final payment.
So on the clasp of the handle, in runic letters,
gleaming and golden, it was exactly engraved,
set forth and said, for whom the sword had been made —
finest of irons — who first it was wrought for,
wreathed at the handle and gleaming with serpents.
Then the wise one spoke (all were silent),

the son of old Healfdene: "He may say without contradiction —
he who performs fairness and truth among his people
(the hoary old ruler remembers the past) —
that this man is better by birth, this child of the nobles!
Your fame is spread through far-off countries,
good friend Beowulf, over all the nations.
You hold it all firmly, hero-like strength joined
with prudence of spirit. I'll prove myself grateful
as we agreed before; you, long granted life, shall
become a great comfort to your kinsmen and comrades,

a help to heroes. Heremod was not
such to the Scyldings, the successors of Ecgwela;
he did not grow to please them, but brought grievous destruction
and dire death-woes upon the Danes;
he slew his table-companions in anger,
trustworthy counselors, until he turned away alone
from the joys of the world, that wide-famed ruler —
though high-ruling heaven had raised him in hero-strength,
had exalted him in might, had made him supreme
over the men of all nations, yet a murderous spirit
grew in his breast. He gave no ring-jewels then
to the Danes by custom; he endured joyless times,
suffering the distress of raging strife,
long-lasting sorrow for his people. Learn from this,
lay hold of virtue! Though laden with winters,
I have sung you these lessons. It is a marvel to tell
how all-ruling God, out of greatness of spirit,
gives wisdom to the children of men,
estate and earlship: He rules all things.
He often allows the thoughts of a man
of illustrious lineage to turn toward possessions,
grants him earthly delights in his home,
a high stronghold of heroes to hold in his keeping,
makes portions of earth-folk obey him,
and a wide-reaching kingdom, so that — wisdom failing him —
he himself is unable to reckon its boundaries.
He lives in luxury; little hinders him,
neither sickness nor age, nor does treachery-sorrow
cloud his spirit; no conflict appears anywhere,
no sword-hate, but all the world goes
as he wishes — he knows nothing worse —
until arrogance, growing within him,
swells and springs up, while the warden is sleeping,
the guard of the soul. Surrounded by sorrows,
his slumber is too sound; the slayer is near him,
who aims with bow and arrow in malice.

chapters.title: Fitt XXVI — Hrothgar Moralizes — Rest After Labor
paragraphs:
"Then, struck in his breast with a bitter-toothed arrow,
he is wounded beneath his helmet: from harmful pollution
he cannot shield himself by the strange commands
of the loathsome-cursed spirit. What he has held too long
seems too little to him; in his savagery he hoards it,
nor gives out gold-plated rings boastfully;
he flouts and forgets the future fate,
since God had already given him no small greatness,
the Wielder of Glory. His end-day near,
it afterwards happens that the body-dwelling
fleetingly fades, falls into ruin;
another takes hold who deals out the ornaments,
the nobleman's jewels, lamenting nothing,
heeding no terror. Oh, dear Beowulf,
best of heroes, defend yourself against evil-strife,
and choose for yourself the better, eternal counsels;

beware of arrogance, world-famous champion!
Only a little while does the fullness of your life-vigor last;
it will soon happen that illness or sword-edge
shall part you from your strength, or the grasp of fire,
or the wave of the current, or the clutch of blade-edges,
or the flight of the war-spear, or age with its horrors,
or your eyes' bright flash shall fade into darkness:
it will happen full early, excellent hero,
that death shall subdue you. So I held the Danes
half a century under heaven, helped them in struggles
against many a race in middle-earth's regions,
with ash-wood and blade-edges, so that no enemies
on earth molested me. Look! a reversing change
came then to my hall, grief after joy,
when Grendel became my constant visitor,
an inveterate hater: from that malice
I continually suffered no small trouble.
Thanks be to God, to the everlasting Lord,
that I gained in my lifetime the chance to look
with my own eyes on the gory head, after long-lasting sorrow!
Go to the bench now, adorned for battle,
joy in the feasting: we'll share many jewels
in common when morning appears."
The Geat was gladdened, went immediately
to the bench, as the wise one bade him.
Then once again, as before, the ones famed for prowess,
the hall's inhabitants, were handsomely banqueted,
feasted anew. The night-veil fell then
dark over the warriors. The courtiers rose then;
the gray-haired one was eager to go to his rest,
the hoary old Scylding. The Geat too
longed greatly for rest,

the doughty champion: a retainer soon led him outside,
wearied from his travels, the man from a far country,
one who for etiquette's sake attended to all
a liegeman's needs, such as seamen at that time
were bound to feel. The big-hearted man rested;
the building towered up, spacious and gilded,
the guest slept inside, until the sable-clad raven
blithely announced the beacon of heaven.
Then the bright-shining sun came moving over the plains;
the warriors hastened, the heads of the peoples
were ready to go again to their own peoples;
the high-minded traveler wished to look far away
for his ship. The valiant one then commanded

Ecglaf's son to bear away Hrunting,
to take back his weapon, his well-beloved iron;
he thanked him for the gift, saying he considered
the war-friend mighty and good, nor did he speak any blame
of the blade: he was a brave-hearted hero.
When the warriors were ready, arrayed in their gear,
the prince dear to the Danes advanced then
onto the dais, where the other was sitting;
the grim-hearted hero greeted King Hrothgar.

chapters.title: Fitt XXVII — Sorrow at Parting
paragraphs:
Beowulf spoke, son of Ecgtheow:
"We seafarers wish to declare now,
come from far lands, that we are firmly determined
to seek King Higelac. We have been welcomed
and feasted here as fittingly as heart could desire;
the greeting was good. If in any way
I can gain more of your affection, ruler of heroes,
than I have yet earned, I shall be quickly ready
for combat and conflict. If, across the ocean's course,
I hear that your neighbors alarm you with terror,
as haters did before, I will bring you
thousands of thanes here to help the heroes.

I know concerning Higelac, the lord of the Geats —
though young in years, he will yet permit me,
by words and by works, as warden of the people,
fully to furnish you with forces and to bear
my lance to your aid, if your liegemen should fail you,
and the help of my hand-strength. If Hrethric,
the king's son, thinks of visiting the Geats' court,
he will find friends there in abundance:
far-off countries are better sought
by one who trusts in himself." Then Hrothgar spoke,
making reply: "All-knowing God
has put these words into your spirit!

Never have I heard a warrior so young in life
more clever in speaking. You are cautious in spirit,
mighty in muscle, prudent in answering.
I count on the hope that, if it ever happens
that a missile shall rob you of Hrethel's descendant,
an edge-fierce battle, and illness or weapon
deprive you of your prince, your people's protector,

and you yet hold your life, the Sea-Geats will never
find a more fitting folk-lord to choose for themselves,
a treasure-ward of heroes, than _you_ might prove —
if you care to govern the kingdom of your kinsmen.
Your spirit pleases me the longer the better,
dear Beowulf: you have brought it about
that peace shall be shared between both these peoples,
the Geats and the Danes; strife shall be suspended,
the secret assaults they suffered in days past;
and so long as I govern the wide-stretching kingdom,
that jewels shall be shared, and that many shall visit
others across the ocean with excellent gift-gems:
the ring-adorned ship shall bring over the currents
presents and love-gifts. These people I know
to be firmly established, toward foe and friend,
blameless in every way by ancient etiquette."
Then the warden of earls, Healfdene's kinsman,
gave him a dozen more jewels,
bade him safely seek his well-beloved people
with these gifts, and return soon.

Then the noble-born king kissed the distinguished,
dear-beloved liegeman; the Dane-prince saluted him
and clasped his neck. Tears fell from him,
from the gray-headed man: he looked for two things,
aged and reverend, but the second more strongly —
that, bold in council, they would meet again.
The man was so dear to him that he could not suppress
the emotions that moved him, but in mood-fetters, fastened

deep in his spirit, the long-famous hero secretly longed
for the dear-beloved man,
though not a blood-kinsman. Beowulf then,
the gold-splendid warrior, walked over the meadows,
exulting in treasure: the sea-going vessel
rode at anchor, awaiting its owner.
As they pressed on their way, Hrothgar's gift

was often spoken of: a folk-king indeed
blameless in every way, until age deprived him
of the joys of his might — as age has often injured many.

chapters.title: Fitt XXVIII — The Homeward Journey — The Two Queens
paragraphs:
Then the band of very valiant retainers
came to the current; they were all clad in armor,

in link-woven mail-coats. The land-warden noticed
the return of the warriors, as he had seen them earlier;
he greeted the strangers with no insult
from the headland of the cliff, but rode on to meet them;
he said that the bright-armored visitors, heading for their ship,
were welcome to the Weders. The wide-bosomed craft then
lay on the sand, loaded with armor,
with horses and jewels — the ring-stemmed vessel:
the mast towered above Hrothgar's treasure.

To the ship-warden Beowulf gave a gold-bound sword,
so that afterwards he was more highly honored on the ale-bench
as owner of that heirloom. Then he set out in his vessel,
to drive on the deep; he left Dane-country behind.
Along the mast a sea-garment fluttered,
a rope-fastened sail. The sea-boat resounded;
the wind over the waters in no way kept
the wave-floater from its journey; the sea-goer traveled,
the foamy-necked floated forth over the currents,
the well-fashioned vessel over the ways of the ocean,

until they came within sight of the Geats' cliffs,
the well-known headlands. The wave-goer hastened,
driven by breezes, and ran up onto the shore.
The harbor-warden was ready at the ocean,
he who had long in the past gazed into the distance,
waiting at the water's edge for his well-loved heroes;
he bound the broad-bosomed vessel to the bank
fast in its cables, lest the force of the waters
could injure the fair ocean-wood.
He bade them bring up the treasure of princes,
the plate-gold and fretwork; it was not far from there
to go in search of the giver of jewels:
Hrethel's son Higelac was at home,
himself with his comrades, close to the sea-coast.
The building was splendid, the king heroic,
great in his hall; Hygd was very young,

fine-minded and clever, though few were the winters
the daughter of Hæreth had dwelt in the stronghold;
yet she was in no way cringing, nor stingy of gifts,
of rare ornaments, to the race of the Geats.

Thrytho, an excellent folk-queen, nursed anger,
hot-burning hatred: no hero whatever
among the household companions, excepting her husband,
dared venture to look at the woman
with his eyes by daylight; for he knew that deadly chains,
hand-wreathed, would be wrought for him: soon afterwards,
once seized, the blade-edges would be ready,
the fierce-raging sword-point would force a decision,
show forth murder-bale. Such is no womanly custom
for a lady to practice, though lovely her person —
that a peace-weaver, on pretense of anger,
should deprive a beloved liegeman of life.
Truly this was hindered by Heming's kinsman;
other ale-drinking warriors asserted
that she worked fewer terrible sorrows upon the people,
fewer treacherous doings, from the time she was first given,
adorned with gold, to the young war-hero,
honored for her lineage, when by her father's instructions
she sought Offa's great palace over the pale flood
on her journey — where afterwards she fully,
famed for her virtue, enjoyed her destined place
on the king's-seat in her lifetime, held love with
the ruler of heroes, the best — so it is told me —
of all earthly men that the oceans encompass,
of endless lineages of earls; hence Offa was famous
far and wide, by gifts and by battles,
the spear-valiant hero; he governed with wisdom
the home of his fathers, from which came Eomær
as help to heroes, Heming's kinsman,
grandson of Garmund, great in combat.

chapters.title: Fitt XXIX — Beowulf and Higelac
paragraphs: Then the brave one departed, his band along with him,

seeking the sea-shore, treading the sea-marches,
the wide-stretching shores. The world-candle glimmered,
the sun from the south; they proceeded on,
arriving soon where they heard that the troop-lord,
Ongentheow's slayer, the excellent, youthful
folk-prince and warrior, was distributing jewels,
close within his castle. The coming of Beowulf
was announced in a message quickly to Higelac,
that the defender of the people was advancing
alive to the palace, the shield-companion,
secure from combat, coming to the court.
The building was soon made ready within
for the guests on foot, as the good one had ordered.
Then Higelac sat beside the man who had survived the struggle,
kinsman by kinsman, after the king of the people
had, in lordly language, saluted the dear one,

in formal words. The daughter of Hæreth
passed through the building, carrying mead-cups:
she loved the retainers, and offered the beakers
to the high-minded Geats. Higelac then began

to ply his companion pleasantly with questions
in the high-towering palace. A curious interest
tormented his spirit — what meaning to find in
the Sea-Geats' adventures: "Worthy Beowulf,

how did your journey fare, when you suddenly resolved
to seek combat far across the salt-streams,
a battle at Heorot? Have you bettered at all
for Hrothgar, the famous folk-leader, his widely known sorrows?
I brooded on torture in billows of anguish,

I distrusted the journey of my beloved liegeman;
I long prayed you by no means to seek out
the murderous spirit, to let the South-Danes themselves
settle the matter by grappling with Grendel.
I thank God that I am allowed to see you
safe from your journey."

Beowulf answered, son of old Ecgtheow:
"It is in no way hidden, chieftain Higelac,
from many men, this famous meeting —
what mournful moments Grendel and I spent
in the place where he brought ruinous affliction,
endless anguish, on the Victory-Scyldings.
All that I avenged, so that none under heaven
of Grendel's kindred need boast of that cry-in-the-morning,
none who longest lives of that loathsome race,
encompassed by moorland. I came on my journey
to the royal ring-hall to greet Hrothgar:

soon the famous son of Healfdene,
when he fully understood the spirit that led me,
assigned me a seat beside his own son.
The troop was in joy; never under the arch of heaven
have I beheld greater mead-gladness

among hall-dwellers. The highly famed queen,
peace-bond of peoples, often passed through the building,
cheered the young troopers; she often handed a hero
a beautiful ring-band before she took her seat.

Often Hrothgar's daughter, in sight of the courtiers,
carried the ale-vessel to the warriors at the far end;
I heard the hall-sitters call her Freaware
when she gave nail-adorned jewels to the heroes:

gold-bedecked, young, her faith has been pledged
to the glad son of Froda; the friend of the Scyldings,
the guardian of the kingdom, has given his consent,
and counts it an advantage — that, for a part of the quarrels,
a portion of the hatred, he should pay with the woman.
It rarely happens, when the ruler has fallen,
that the life-taking lance relaxes its fury
for even a brief breathing-space, though the bride be charming!

chapters.title: Fitt XXX — Beowulf Narrates His Adventures to Higelac
paragraphs:
"It may well disturb the prince of the Heathobards
and each of the thanes who attend on his earls,
when he goes into the hall escorting the woman,
that a noble-born Dane is being feasted among the knights:
on that Dane gleam the heirlooms of elders,
hard and ring-bright, treasures of the Heathobards,
which they once wielded as arms, until they led to ruin
their own dear lives and beloved companions.
At the banquet someone who sees the collar speaks,
an old ash-warrior who clearly recalls
the death of his countrymen (cruel is his spirit),
and sadly begins to sound out the young
thane-champion's feelings through the thoughts of his breast,
to wake war-grief, and he says these words:
'Can you, my friend, recognize it when you see it,
the blade your father bore to battle
in his last venture, under his helmet's visor,
the dearly loved iron, where the Danes slew him
and brave-minded Scyldings — after the fall of the heroes,
when vengeance was sleeping — held the slaughter-field?
And now some man of the murderer's line,
exulting in ornaments, enters the building,
boasts of his bloodshed, carries off the jewel
that you should rightfully possess!'
So he urges and reminds him at every chance
with woe-bringing words, until the time comes
when the woman's thane, for the deeds of his father,
sleeps bloody-gory, the blade having bitten him,
fated to die; the other one escapes
from there alive — he knows the country thoroughly.
Then the oaths of the warriors on both sides are broken,
as unresting rancors rage in Ingeld,
and his love for his wife grows less warm after sorrow.
So I do not reckon the Heathobards' goodwill faithful,
their part in the treaty not true to the Danes,
their friendship not firm. I shall tell you further

about Grendel, so that you may fully hear,
ornament-giver, what afterwards came of
the hand-rush of the heroes. When heaven's bright jewel
had glided across earth's fields, the stranger came raging,
the horrible night-fiend, to visit us
where we were guarding the hall entirely unharmed.

A hopeless struggle came upon Hondscio,
death to the doomed one; girded war-champion,
he fell first, dead. To that distinguished vassal,
Grendel became a tooth-weaponed murderer,
and swallowed the well-beloved henchman's body whole.
Yet the bloody-toothed murderer, mindful of evils,
was not the sooner going to escape empty-handed
from the gold-giver's palace;
sturdy of strength, he tried to outdo me,
grappled me with a ready hand. A glove was hanging there,
spacious and wondrous, fastened with cunning fetters,
which had been fashioned entirely by the craftsman's touch
from the dragon's skin, by the devil's devices:
there, in its depths, the raging deed-doer
meant to place me, unjustly, among many others,
though he saw that I was without sin; but so it could not be,
when I in my anger stood upright.
It is too long to recount how I furnished requital
for every evil to the destroyer of warriors;

it was there, my prince, that I proudly distinguished
your land by my labors. He turned and retreated,
lived his life a little while longer:
yet his right arm was left behind to guard his trail in Heorot,
and sad-minded he fell from there to the sea-bottom,
mournful in mind. For the might-rush of battle

the friend of the Scyldings repaid me much,
with gold-plated treasure and many ornaments,
when daylight had dawned, and we had sat down
together at the banquet. There was singing and joy:
the age-stricken Scylding asked many questions
and spoke of old times; often the brave one touched
the light-ringing harp-strings, the joy-telling wood;
sometimes he uttered measures mournful and true,
then the large-hearted land-king told us truthfully
a legend of wonder. And sometimes, troubled with years,

the age-hoary warrior would then begin
to mourn for the might that marked him in his youth-days;
his breast boiled within when, burdened with winters,
he remembered much. From morning till night
we joyed ourselves as etiquette allowed,
until the second night came upon earth-folk.
Then soon afterwards, Grendel's mother
was ready for vengeance; wretched she journeyed;
death had ravished her son — the wrath of the Geats.
The horrible woman avenged her offspring,
and with mighty main-strength murdered a hero.

There the spirit of Æschere, aged counselor,
was ready to depart; nor when morning had lightened
were the people of the Danes permitted in any way
to consume the death-weakened hero with fire,
nor to lay their beloved liegeman on the pyre;

she had carried the corpse away in the foe's clutches
under the mountain-brook's flood. To Hrothgar this was the saddest
of all the pains that had ever preyed on the chieftain;
by your life the land-prince then sadly besought me
to display my prowess in the eddies of the sea-currents,
to put my safety in peril,
to accomplish deeds of might; and much did he promise.

I found there the famous flood-current's cruel,
horrible depth-warden. For a while the two of us
were hand-to-hand; the currents were seething
with clotted gore, and Grendel's fierce mother's
head I hacked off in the hall at the bottom
with a huge-reaching sword-edge; hardly did I wrest
my life from her clutches; but I was not yet doomed,

for the warden of warriors afterwards gave me
jewels in plenty, the kinsman of Healfdene.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXI — Gift-giving is Mutual
paragraphs:
"So the beloved land-prince lived with honor;
I had missed no rewards, no payments for my prowess,
but he gave me jewels according to my wishes,
he, Healfdene's son; so I shall bring them to you,
prince of warriors, and offer them gladly.
And still all my affection belongs to you:
I find few of my kin surviving
but you, dear Higelac!" Then he bade them bring in
the boar-image, the banner, the battle-high helmet,
the iron-gray armor, the excellent weapon,

and said in song-measures: "Hrothgar presented me
this battle-dress, and expressly bade me,
the wise-minded prince, to tell you afterwards
the whole of its history: he said that King Heregar
had owned it, the Dane-prince, for a long time; yet he did not wish
to give the mail to his son, though he loved him dearly —
Hereward the hardy. Keep it all in joy!"
I heard that hard upon the jewels there followed
two pairs of stallions of striking resemblance,
dappled and yellow; he granted him possession
of horses and treasures. So a kinsman should bear himself,
weave no web of treachery for another,
nor by cunning craftiness cause the destruction

of a trusty companion. To Higelac,
the one bold in battle, his sister's son was most precious,
and each was mindful of favors to the other.

I am told that to Hygd he presented the necklace,
the rare wonder-gem that Wealhtheow had given him,
the troop-leader's daughter, along with three horses
slender and saddle-bright; soon did the jewel
adorn her bosom, once the beer-feast was over.
So the son of Ecgtheow proved himself brave,

a war-famous man, by valiant deeds,
he lived in honor, slew no beloved
companions in carousing; his mood was not cruel,
but by hand-strength, the mightiest of heroes then living,
the brave one kept faithfully the generous gift
that the Lord had allowed him. Long had he been wretched,
so that the sons of the Geats had accounted him worthless,
and the lord of the liegemen was loath to grant him
much honor when the mead-cups were being passed;
they fully believed him to be idle and sluggish,

an indolent prince: but to the honor-blessed man
came payment for the slights he had suffered.
The folk-troop's defender bade them fetch to the hall
the heirloom of Hrethel, embellished with gold,

as the brave one ordered; there was no richer jewel
in the form of a weapon among the Geats of that era;
he placed it in Beowulf's keeping, and gave him
seven thousand hides, a hall and lordship.
Land was held in common by both among the people,
estate and inherited rights and possessions,
but more especially a spacious domain
to the one who was higher ranking. It afterwards happened
in the days that followed, it befell the battle-thanes,

after Higelac's death, and when Heardred was murdered
with weapons of war beneath well-covered shields —
when valiant battle-men sought him out in victor-band,
War-Scylfing heroes harassed in battle
the nephew of Hereric — then in time
extensive dominions turned to Beowulf's keeping:

he ruled them fittingly for fifty winters
(he was a wise man-ruler, an old manor-ward), until
a certain one began, on gloom-darkening nights,
a dragon, to rule — one who guarded a treasure,
a high-rising stone-cliff on a grayish heath:
a path lay beneath it, unknown to mortals.
Some man entered the mountain,
and eagerly laid hold of the heathen hoard;

chapters.title: Fitt XXXII — The Hoard and the Dragon
paragraphs:
He did not go there of his own will, the one who sorely harmed him;
rather, under pressing need, the servant of one of
the heroes' sons was fleeing hate-blows,
seeking for shelter, and the sin-driven man
took refuge inside. He looked around early,

*  *  *  *  *  * when the onset surprised him,
he saw a gem-vessel there: many such
ancient ornaments lay in the earth-cave,
as long ago some man of illustrious lineage
had secreted them there, a monstrous legacy,
careful and thoughtful, with dear-valued jewels.
Death had carried them off in days past,
and the one man moreover — the last of the flower
of that people — who had stayed the longest,
a friend-mourning guardian, was eager to defer it
a little longer, to be left in the enjoyment
of his long-lasting treasure. A barrow, all ready,
stood on the plain near the stream-currents,
new by the headland's edge, hard to approach:
the keeper of rings carried inside
a ponderous share of the nobles' treasure,
of beaten gold, and spoke briefly then:

"Hold now, O Earth, what heroes no longer can,
the earnings of warriors. Look! long ago in your bosom
worthy men won these things; war-death has ravished —
perilous life-bale — all my warriors,
beloved liegemen, who have forsaken this life,
who saw the pleasures of the hall. I have no sword-bearer,
no one to burnish the gold-plated vessel,
the high-valued beaker: my heroes are vanished.
The hardy helmet, hung with gilding,
shall be stripped of its riches: the ring-cleaners sleep
who were charged with keeping battle-visors ready,
and the mail-coat that endured in battle-encounters
over the breaking of war-shields, under the bite of edges,
moulders with its hero. The ring-twisted armor,
its lord being lifeless, can no longer travel
hung on heroes; harp-joy is vanished,
the rapture of the glee-wood, no excellent falcon
swoops through the hall, no swift-footed charger
grinds the gravel. A grievous destruction
has widely scattered no few of the world's people!"
So, woeful in spirit, the last one left
lamented mournfully, moaning in sadness
by day and by night, until death with its billows

dashed upon his spirit. Then the ancient dusk-scather
found the great treasure standing wide open,
he who, flaming and fiery, flies to the barrows —
the naked war-dragon who by night escapes
encompassed with fire; men under heaven
beheld him widely. It is said that he looks for
the hoard in the earth, where, old, he guards
the heathen treasure; he will be no better for it.

So for three hundred winters the waster of peoples
held on earth that excellent hoard-hall,
until the aforementioned man angered him bitterly:
he bore the beaten-plated beaker to his chieftain
and begged of his liege-lord full remission
for all his offenses. Then the hoard was uncovered,
the treasure was taken, his petition was granted

to the downcast liegeman. His lord looked on
the old work of earth-folk — it was the first such occasion.
When the dragon awoke, strife was renewed there;
he sniffed along the stone then, and stout-hearted found
the footprint of the foe; too close he had gone,
with cunning craftiness, to the fire-spewing dragon's head.
So may an undoomed man easily escape
anguish and exile, if he possesses
the favor of Heaven. The hoard-warden then eagerly
searched over the ground; he wanted to find the person
who had caused him sorrow while he lay in slumber:
gleaming and wild, he often went round the cavern,
all of it outward; but not one of men
was to be seen in that desert. Yet he rejoiced in the coming fight,
took joy in the conflict: often he turned to the barrow,
sought for the gem-cup; and soon he perceived
that some man or other had discovered the gold,
the famous folk-treasure. The hoard-ward was not content
to wait until evening; then the guardian of the barrow
was angry in spirit, the loathsome one wished
to pay back for the dear-valued drink-cup with fire.
Then the day was done, as the dragon would have it;
he would no longer wait on the wall, but departed

fire-driven, flaming. Fearful was the onset
for the warriors in the land, as soon afterwards
it was grievously ended for their gold-giver.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXIII — Brave Though Aged — Reminiscences
paragraphs:
Then the stranger began to spew out fire,
to burn the great manor; the blaze flickered
bringing anguish to the earls — the hateful air-flier
was unwilling to leave anything living behind.
The war of the worm was widely noticed,
the feud of the foe near and far,
how the enemy injured the earls of the Geats,
harrying them with hatred. Then back he hurried to his treasure,
to the well-hidden cavern before daybreak.
He had circled the folk of those regions with fire,
with brand and burning; in the barrow he trusted,
in its walls and his war-might — but the weening deceived him.

Then the horror was at once made known to Beowulf,
told to him truly: that his own native homestead,
the best of buildings, was burning and melting,
the gift-seat of the Geats. It was a grief to the spirit
of the good-minded hero, the greatest of sorrows.

The wise one thought then that, in wielding his kingdom,
he had bitterly angered the everlasting Lord
against the ancient commandments; with mournful meditations
his breast welled inward, as was nowise his custom.
The fire-spewing dragon had fully wasted
the fastness of the warriors, the water-land outward,
the manor with fire. The folk-ruling hero,
prince of the Weders, was planning to wreak vengeance.
The defender of warmen, atheling of earls,
bade them make for him an excellent war-shield

wholly of iron: he knew full well
that wood from the forest was helpless to aid him,
no shield against fire. The long-worthy ruler
must live out the last of his limited earth-days,
of life in the world, and the worm along with him,
though he had long been holding hoard-wealth in plenty.

Then the ring-prince disdained to seek the air-going ranger
with a war-band, with an army extensive;
he felt no fear of the foeman's assaults,
and he counted for little the might of the dragon,
his power and prowess — for previously he had dared

a heap of hostilities, hazarded many dangers,
war-thane, when he cleansed Hrothgar's palace,
conquering combatant, and clutched in the battle
the kinsmen of Grendel, of kindred detested.

It was not least of his hand-fights where Higelac was slaughtered,
when the king of the Geats, in the clash of battle,
friend-lord of folk in the Frisian dominions,
offspring of Hrethel, perished through sword-drink,
beaten down with battle-swords. From there Beowulf came,
relying on his own strength, swam through the waters;
he bore on his arm, traveling alone, thirty
outfits of armor when he climbed out of the ocean.
The Hetwars had no cause to be boastful
of their fighting afoot, who carried their war-shields
forward to meet him: not many returned
from the brave-minded battle-knight back to their homesteads.
Ecgtheow's son then swam over the bight-courses,
a lone-goer returning sorrowful to his land-folk,
where Hygd offered him treasure and kingdom,

rings and dominion: she did not trust her son
to be able to keep the kingdom devised for him
against alien races, upon the death of King Higelac.

Yet the sad ones in no way succeeded in persuading the atheling
to act in any fashion as suzerain
over Heardred, or to promise to govern the kingdom;
yet with friendly counsel he sustained him among the folk,
gracious, with honor, until he grew older

and wielded the Weders. Wide-fleeing outlaws,
Ohthere's sons, sought him out over the waters:
they had stirred revolt against the helm of the Scylfings,
the best of sea-kings, who in Swedish dominions
distributed treasure, a distinguished folk-leader.
That was the end of Heardred's earth-days; fatal injury
by swing of the sword he received as a greeting,
the offspring of Higelac; Ongentheow's son
afterward departed to visit his homestead,
when Heardred was dead; he let Beowulf rule them,
govern the Geats — good was that folk-king.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXIV — Beowulf Seeks the Dragon — Beowulf's Reminiscences
paragraphs:
He planned requital for the folk-leader's ruin
in the days thereafter, becoming an enemy
to Eadgils the wretched. Ohthere's son then
went with a war-troop over the wide-stretching currents,
with warriors and weapons; afterward, in cold woe-journeys,
he avenged himself — he took the king's life.

So he came off uninjured from all of his battles,
the perilous fights, the offspring of Ecgtheow,
from his deeds of daring, until that most momentous day
when he, fate-driven, went forth to fight with the dragon.

With eleven companions the prince of the Geats
went lowering with fury to look upon the fire-drake:
by inquiring he had learned how the feud had arisen,
this hate against his heroes; the highly-famed gem-vessel
was brought into his keeping through the hand of the informer.

The thirteenth man in that throng of heroes,
the one who had caused the beginning of this bitter conflict,
a captive and wretched, sad-minded, had now

to point out the place: he passed on unwillingly
to the spot where he knew the notable cavern lay,
the cave under the earth, not far from the ocean,
the anger of the eddies, which was full within
of jewels and wires: an uncanny warden,
a weaponed warrior, guarded the treasure,
old under the earth; no easy possession
for any of earth-folk to gain access to.
Then the battle-brave atheling sat on the naze-edge,
while the gold-friend of the Geats graciously saluted
his hearth-companions: his spirit was woeful,
death-boding, wavering; Weird was very near him,
she who must seize the old hero, seek out his soul-treasure,
dragging his life apart from his body:
not much longer would the folk-leader's spirit be flesh-hidden.
Beowulf spoke, Ecgtheow's son:
"In my youth-days I survived many a conflict,
many hours of onset: I remember them all.
I was seven winters old when the jewel-prince took me,
high-lord of heroes, from the hands of my father;
Hrethel the hero-king had me in keeping,
gave me treasure and feasting, remembered our kinship;
I was not ever any less dear to him,

as a knight in the boroughs, than the sons of his own household —
Herebald and Hæthcyn and my Higelac.
For the eldest, unjustly, by the acts of a kinsman,
was a murder-bed strewn, since Hæthcyn from his horn-bow

struck down his sheltering chieftain with an arrow,
erred in his aim and injured his kinsman,
one brother the other, with a blood-sprinkled spear:

It was a fight no fine could settle, finished in malice,
sad to his spirit; the folk-prince nevertheless
had to depart from existence with his vengeance untaken.

So it is heavily crushing to a hoar-headed hero
to live to see his son riding
young on the gallows: then he chants his measures,
a song of sorrow, while his son is hanging
for the raven's delight, and he, aged and hoary,
is unable to offer any assistance.
Every morning he is constantly reminded
of his offspring's departure: he cares not to wait
for the birth of another heir in his borough-enclosures,
since that one, through death-pain, has already experienced its deeds.
Heart-grieved, he beholds in his son's house
the wine-building wasted, the wind-lodging places
reaved of their roaring; the riders are sleeping,
the knights in the grave; there is no sound of the harp-wood,
no joy in the yards, as once was familiar.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXV — Reminiscences (continued) — Beowulf's Last Battle
paragraphs:
"He then seeks his chamber and sings a woe-song,
one man for another; the homesteads and plains
seemed all too vast and empty. So the helm of the Weders

mindful of Herebald, carried heart-sorrow,
stirred with emotion, and was nowise able
to wreak ruin on the ruthless destroyer:
he could not pursue the warrior with hatred,
with direful deeds, though he no longer held him dear.
Then, pressed by the pang that this pain gave him,
he gave up gladness, chose God's light;
he left to his sons, as a rich man does,
his land and fortress when he departed from life.

Then there was crime and hostility between Swedes and Geats,
warring was mutual across the wide-stretching water,
a burdensome hatred, once Hrethel had perished,
and Ongentheow's offspring were active and valiant —
they did not wish to keep peace oversea, but
round Hreosna-beorh they often accomplished
the cruelest massacre. This my kinsman avenged,
the feud and fury, as is found on inquiry,
though one of them paid for it with the forfeit of life-joys,

with a hard price: the struggle became then
fatal to Hæthcyn, lord of the Geats.
Then I heard that at morning one brother urged on the other
to murder with the edges of irons,
when Ongentheow made his onset on Eofor:
the helmet crashed, the hoary-haired Scylfing
fell sword-smitten, his hand remembering
feud-hate enough — it did not refuse the death-blow.
The gems Hrethel gave me, with my jewel-bright sword
I repaid him in contest, as occasion offered:
he granted me land, life-joy at the homestead,
a manor to live on. Little did he need
to look among Gepids or Danes or in Sweden
for any less true a trooper, to buy with treasure;
among foot-soldiers I would always press out in front,
alone in the vanguard, and will evermore gladly
wage warfare, as long as this weapon endures
that late and early has often served me
since I proved before heroes the slayer of Dæghrefn,
knight of the Hugs: by no means was he allowed
to carry the jewels to the king of the Frisians,
the breast-decoration; but the banner-bearer
bowed in the battle, that brave-minded atheling.
No weapon was his slayer — war-grapple broke then
the surge of his spirit, destroying his body.
Now shall the weapon's edge make war for the treasure,
and hand and firm sword." Beowulf spoke then,
uttered boast-words — for the latest occasion:
"I braved in my youth-days battles unnumbered;
still am I willing to look for the struggle,
to perform fame-deeds, a prudent folk-warden,
if the hateful despoiler seeks me out
from his cavern!" Each of the heroes,
the sturdy helm-bearers, he thereupon greeted,

his beloved co-liegemen — this his last salutation:
"No brand would I bear, no blade for the dragon,
if I knew any way to accomplish my word-boast
against the monster otherwise, as I did with Grendel;
but here I expect hot fire in the battle,
furious flame-burning: so I fixed on my body
both targe and war-mail. The ward of the barrow
I will not flee from by a foot-length, the foeman uncanny.
At the wall it will befall us as Fate decrees,
each one's Creator. I am eager in spirit,
ready to leave off all boasting with the wingèd war-hero.
Wait on the barrow, protected by byrnies,

earls in armor — to see which of us two may better
bear his disaster, when the battle is over.
It is no matter of yours, and no man can do it,
but me and me only, to measure strength with
the monster of malice, to accomplish mighty deeds.
I with prowess shall gain the gold, or else the battle,
a direful death-woe, will drag off your ruler!"
The mighty champion rose then by his shield,
brave under helmet; in battle-mail he went
beneath the steep-rising stone-cliffs, relying on the strength
of one man alone: no work for a coward.
Then he saw by the wall, one who had lived through
a great many battles, most worthy, when foot-troops collided,

the stone-arches standing, the stout-hearted champion,
and saw a brook bubbling forth from the barrow:
the flood of that fountain was fuming with war-flame;
he could not, for even the briefest season,
brave without burning the abyss that was yawning near the hoard,
so fiery was the drake. The prince of the Weders
then caused words to come forth from his bosom,
so fierce was his fury; the firm-hearted shouted:
his battle-clear voice came resounding
beneath the gray-colored stone. Stirred was his hatred;

the hoard-ward made out the speech of a man;
there was no longer time to look out for friendship.
The breath of the monster issued forth first,
a vapory war-sweat, out of the stone-cave:
the earth re-echoed. The earl beneath the barrow
lifted his shield, the lord of the Geats,
toward the terrible stranger: the ring-twisted creature's
heart was then ready to seek for a struggle.

The lord of the troopers intrepidly stood
behind his high-rising shield, when the dragon coiled

quickly together: in corslet he waited.
Then the dragon went in blazes, bending and striding,
hastening forward. His life and body
the targe protected well, but for a shorter time
than the well-renowned leader would have wished,
there, where for the first day he was forced to be victor,
famous in battle, since Fate had not willed otherwise.
The lord of the Geats then uplifted his hand,
smiting the fire-drake with his precious sword,
so that the blade-edge weakened bright on the bone,
bit more feebly than his folk-leader needed,
burdened as he was with bale-griefs. Then the barrow-protector,

when the sword-blow had fallen, was fierce in his spirit,
flinging his fires; the flamings of battle
gleamed afar: the gold-friend of the Weders

boasted no conquests — his battle-sword failed him
naked in conflict, as it by no means ought to,
that long-trusty weapon. It was no slight undertaking
that Ecgtheow's famous offspring would leave
the drake-cavern's bottom; he must live in some region
other than this, by the will of the dragon,
as each earth-man must at some point forfeit existence.
It was early thereafter the excellent warriors

met with each other. Anew and afresh
the hoard-ward took heart (gasps heaved then his bosom):

he suffered sorrow, encircled with fire,
he who had governed the people before. His companions
were in no way banded about him, those sons of the princes,

with valorous spirit; they fled instead to the forest,
seeking for safety. The soul-deeps of one among them
were

ruffled by care: kin-love can never
waver in him who considers well.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXVI — Wiglaf the Trusty — Beowulf is Deserted by Friends and by Sword
paragraphs:
The son of Weohstan was named Wiglaf,
precious shield-warrior, prince of the Scylfings,
Ælfhere's kinsman: he saw his dear liegelord
enduring the heat beneath his helmet and visor.
Then he minded the holding that had earlier been given him,

the wealth-blessed homestead of the Wægmunding warriors,
each of the folk-rights his father had wielded;
he grew hot for the battle, his hand seized the targe,
the yellow-bark shield; he unsheathed his old weapon,
which was known among earth-men as the relic of Eanmund,
Ohthere's offspring — whom, exiled and friendless,
Weohstan had slain with sword-edge in battle,
and carried back to his own kinsman the clear-shining helmet,
the ring-made byrnie, the old giant-weapon
that Onela had given him, his boon-fellow's armor,
the ready war-trappings: he did not mention the feud,
though he had fatally smitten the son of his brother.
Many a half-year he held those treasures,
the bill and the byrnie, until his son became able,
like his father before him, to accomplish fame-deeds;
then he gave him, among the Geats, a goodly array
of gear for his warfare; then, old, he went from life
on his journey. It was the earliest time now

that the youthful champion might charge in the battle
at the side of his liegelord; his spirit was dauntless.
Nor did his kinsman's bequest quail in the battle:
this the dragon discovered when they came together.
Wiglaf uttered many a right saying,
spoke to his fellows, sad was his spirit:
"I remember the time when, tasting the mead-cup,
we promised in the hall to the lord of us all
who gave us these ring-treasures, that we would surely repay him
for this battle-equipment, swords and helmets,
should need of such aid ever befall him:
it was for this journey that he chose us in his war-band,
of his own accord, stirred us to glory and gave me these jewels,
since he held and esteemed us trustworthy spearmen,
hardy helm-bearers — though this hero-achievement
our lord intended to accomplish alone,
as warden of his people, for he had done most of the achievements,
the audacious deeds, among earth-folk.

The day is now come when the ruler of earth-men
needs the vigor of valiant heroes:
let us go toward him, to succor the war-prince,
while the heat yet rages, this horrible fire-fight.

God knows in me it is far more pleasing
that the blaze should embrace my body and eat it
alongside my treasure-bestower. It seems not proper
to bear our battle-shields back to our country
unless first we are able to fell and destroy
the long-hating foeman, and to defend the life of

the prince of the Weders. Well do I know it is not
earned by his exploits that he alone of the Geats
should suffer sorrow and sink in the battle:
brand and helmet shall be common to us both,
shield-cover, byrnie." Through the bale-smoke he stalked then,
went under helmet to the help of his chieftain,

briefly discoursing: "Beloved Beowulf,
perform now all fully, as you formerly said
in your youthful years, that while yet you lived
you would let your honor never be lessened.
You shall save your life, mighty in actions,
undaunted atheling, with all of your vigor;

I will give you assistance." The dragon came raging,
the wild-minded stranger, when these words had been uttered
(it was the second occasion), seeking his enemies,
the men who were hated, with hot-gleaming fire-waves;
with blaze-billows burned the board to its edges:
the fight-armor then failed to furnish assistance
to the youthful spear-hero: but the young-aged stripling
quickly advanced beneath his kinsman's war-targe,
since his own had been ground to ashes in the grip of the fire.

brand of Beowulf deceived him in the battle.
It was denied him that edges of iron were able
to help him in the fight; his hand was too mighty,
the hand which — as I heard on inquiry — outstruck
every weapon in its stroke when he carried
to the struggle that wonderful war-sword: it availed him no better.

Then the people-despoiler — in the third of his onsets —
the fierce-raging fire-drake, mindful of his feud-hate,
charged on the strong one when a chance was afforded,
heated and war-grim, and seized him by the neck
with bitter teeth; he grew bloody
with soul-gore seething; sword-blood boiled in waves.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXVII — The Fatal Struggle — Beowulf's Last Moments
paragraphs:
Then I heard that, at the need of the king of the people,
the upstanding earl-man exhibited prowess,
vigor and courage, as suited his nature;
he did not guard his own head, but the high-minded liegeman's
hand was consumed while he succored his kinsman,
as he struck the strife-bringing stranger lower down,
this earl-thane in armor, so that the weapon,
gleaming and plated, went in — and from then on the fire

began to lessen. The liegelord himself then
retained his consciousness, brandished his war-knife,
battle-sharp, bitter, which he bore on his armor:

the Weder-lord cut the worm in the middle.
They had felled the enemy (puissant prowess
had driven out its life), the pair had destroyed him,
related land-chiefs together: so a liegeman should prove himself,
a thane when needed. To the prince this was the last
of his era of conquest by his own great achievements,

the latest of world-deeds. The wound then began
which the earth-dwelling dragon had earlier wrought him
to burn and to swell. He soon discovered
that the bitterest bale-woe was raging in his bosom,
poison within. Then the atheling advanced,

so that, along by the wall, prudent of spirit,
he might sit on a settle; he saw the giant-work,
how arches of stone, strengthened with pillars,
supported from within the eternal earth-hall.
Then the long-worthy liegeman laved with his hand the

far-famous chieftain, gory from sword-edge,
refreshing the face of his friend-lord and ruler,
sated with battle, unbinding his helmet.
Beowulf answered, spoke of his injury,
his wound that was fatal (he was fully aware
that he had lived his allotted life-days, enjoying
the pleasures of earth; now his measure of days
was entirely past, and death very near):

"To my son I would now give my battle-equipment,
had any heir been granted after me,
sprung from my body. This people I have governed
fifty winters: no king among my neighbors
dared to encounter me with comrades-in-battle,
or try me with terror. The time appointed me
I bided at home, kept my own fitly,
sought no snares, nor swore many

oaths in injustice. Joy in all of this
I am able to have, though ill with my death-wounds;
hence the Ruler of Earth-men need not charge me
with the killing of kinsmen, when my life goes out
forth from my body. Go now with haste,

beloved Wiglaf, to behold the hoard
beneath the hoar-gray stone, now that the worm is lying,
sore-wounded, sleeping, dispossessed of his treasure.
Go in haste, so that I may gaze on the ancient treasures,
the gold-wealth, see together the ether-bright jewels
lying there, and, having the heap of hoard-gems,
be the more easily able to yield up
my life and the land-folk whom I long have governed."

chapters.title: Fitt XXXVIII — Wiglaf Plunders the Dragon's Den — Beowulf's Death
paragraphs:
Then I heard that Wihstan's son very quickly,
once these words had been uttered, heeded his liegelord,
wounded and war-sick; he went in his armor,
his well-woven ring-mail, beneath the roof of the barrow.
Then the trusty retainer, victorious,

saw many treasure-gems when he came near to the seat,
gold-treasure sparkling, spread on the bottom,
a wonder on the wall, and the worm-creature's cavern,
the ancient dawn-flier's, with vessels standing,
cups of the ancients bereft of their cleansers,
robbed of their ornaments: there were helmets in number,
old and rust-eaten, many arm-bracelets
artfully woven. Wealth can easily,
gold on the sea-bottom, turn to vanity
any one of earth-men — let arm himself who pleases!
And he saw there, lying high above the hoard,
an all-golden banner, greatest of hand-wonders,
linked with lacets: a light sparkled from it,
so that he was able to look on the floor of the cavern,
to examine the jewels. No sight of the dragon
was offered, for the edge had carried him off.

Then I heard that the hero plundered the hoard-treasure,
reaved the ancient giant-work there in the cavern,
bore on his bosom the beakers and platters,
such as he himself wished, and took off the standard,
the brightest of beacons; the bill had earlier injured
(its edge was of iron) the old ruler's weapon,
the one who had long watched as ward of the jewels,
who had carried fire-terror, hot for the treasure,
rolling in battle, in the middlemost darkness,
until, murdered, he perished. The messenger hastened,
not loath to return, hurried by the jewels:
curiosity urged him, wondering whether, excellent-minded,
he would find the lord of the Weders alive,
mortally wounded, at the place where he had left him.
Among the jewels he then found the famous old chieftain,
his beloved liegelord, at his life's end, gory:
thereupon he began to lave him with water,
until the point of his word pierced through his breast-hoard.
Beowulf spoke (he had noticed the gold-gems),

the old one in sorrow: "For the jewels I look upon
I utter thanks for all to the Ruler,
Wielder of Worship, with words of devotion,
the Lord everlasting, that He let me gain such treasures
for my people before death overtook me.
Since I have bartered the aged life granted me
for this treasure of jewels, attend ye from now on

to the wants of the war-thanes; I can wait here no longer.
Bid the battle-famed build them a grave-hill,
bright when I am burned, at the brim-current's limit;
as a memorial to the men I have governed,
it shall tower aloft, rising upon Whale's-Ness,
so that earls of the ocean may hereafter call it
Beowulf's barrow — those who drive their ever-dashing barks
from afar over the darkness of the waters."

The bold-minded troop-lord took from his neck then
the ring that was golden, gave to his liegeman,
the youthful war-hero, his gold-flashing helmet,
his collar and war-mail, and bade him enjoy them well:
"You are the latest left of the line of our kindred,
of the Wægmunding people: Weird has carried off
all of my kinsmen to the Creator's glory,
earls in their vigor: I shall fare after them."
That was the aged liegelord's last-spoken word
in the musings of his spirit, before he mounted the fire,
the burning battle-waves: from his bosom departed
his soul, to seek the glory of the sainted ones.

chapters.title: Fitt XXXIX — The Dead Foes — Wiglaf's Bitter Taunts
paragraphs:
It had chanced then woefully for the youthful retainer
to behold on earth the one most ardently beloved
at his life-days' limit, lying there helpless.
The slayer too lay there, of all life bereft,
the horrible earth-drake, harassed with sorrow:

the round-twisted monster was permitted no longer
to govern the ring-hoards, for the edges of war-swords,
battle-sharp and sturdy, leavings of hammers,
had mightily seized him, so that, still bleeding from his wounds,
the flier-from-far-land fell to the earth
hard by his hoard-house; no longer did he hop
through the air at midnight, nor, exulting in jewels,
suffer any to see him: he sank then to earth
through the hero-chief's handwork. I heard for certain
that few in the land, liegemen of valor,
have thrived by it — though of every achievement bold
he had proven himself — to run against the breath
of the venomous scather, or to trouble the hall of treasure
with hand-blows, if he had found the ward of the hoard-hall
awake on the barrow. Beowulf's part
of the treasure of jewels was paid for with death;
each of the two had attained the end
of his unlasting life. Not long was it until

the tardy-at-battle returned from the thicket,
the timid truce-breakers, ten all together,
who had not dared before to play with the lances
in their people's prince's pressing emergency;

but blushing with shame, they bore their shields,
with arms and armor, to where the old one was lying:
they gazed upon Wiglaf. He was sitting exhausted,
a foot-going fighter, not far from the shoulders
of the lord of the people; he would rouse him with water;
but it did not help him at all — though he hoped for it keenly,
he was in no way able to retain life in his leader
on earth, nor in any way to alter
the will of the Wielder; the World-Ruler's power
would govern the actions of each one of heroes,

as He still does. From the young one, forthwith,
a grim-worded greeting could quickly be given
to the man whose courage had failed him. Wiglaf spoke then,
Weohstan's son, a sad-minded hero,

looked on the hated ones: "Whoever will speak the truth
can say that the liegelord who gave you these jewels,
the ornament-armor in which you are standing —
when often on the ale-bench he offered to hall-men,
the prince to his liegemen, both helmet and byrnie,
the best that he was able to find upon earth —

that he wasted his war-gear wildly and to no purpose
when battle overtook him. The troop-king had no cause
to glory in those comrades; yet God permitted him,

the Victory-Wielder, unaided with weapon,
to avenge himself, when vigor was needed.
I was able to give him but little life-protection
in the battle, and yet I began, notwithstanding,
to help my kinsman — overtaxing my strength:
he grew the weaker when I struck my mortal opponent
with a weapon, and the fire flamed less strongly
from his bosom. Too few of protectors
came round the king at the critical moment.
Now the giving of ornaments and bestowing of weapons,
all home-joyance, must cease for your kindred,
all food for your people; each of your warriors
must needs be bereft of the rights he holds
in landed possessions, when faraway nobles
shall learn of your leaving your lord so basely,

this dastardly deed. Death is more pleasant
to every earl-man than a life of infamy!"

chapters.title: Fitt XL — The Messenger of Death
paragraphs:
Then he charged that the battle be announced at the hedge
up over the cliff-edge, where the earl-troopers had waited
the whole of the morning, sitting mood-wretched,
bearers of battle-shields, expecting both outcomes —
the end of his lifetime and the coming again
of their beloved liegelord. He held back little
of the news that was known, he who traveled the ness-cliff,
but truly discoursed to all that could hear him:

"Now the free-giving friend-lord of the folk of the Weders,
the folk-prince of the Geats, is fast in his death-bed;
by the deeds of the dragon he abides in his death-bed;
along with him lies his life-taking foeman,
slain with knife-wounds: he was wholly unable
to injure the ill-planning monster at all
with the bite of his sword-edge. Wiglaf is sitting,
the offspring of Wihstan, up over Beowulf,
one earl over another whose end-day has reached him,
holding head-watch over heroes no longer living,

for friend and for foeman. The folk now expect
a season of strife, once the death of the folk-king
is published among the Frankmen and Frisians in far lands.
The war-hatred grew warm against the Hugs

when Higelac came with a fleet of vessels
faring to Friesland, where the Frankmen in battle
humbled him and bravely, by overwhelming might, accomplished
that the mail-clad warrior must sink in the battle,
fallen among his folk-troop: no chased gems did the atheling
present to his earlmen; Merewing's mercy
was ever denied us. For truce or for truth
I trust the men of the Swede-lands but little;
but it was widely known that near Ravenswood Ongentheow

sundered Hæthcyn the Hrethling from life-joys,
when, in their overweening pride, the War-Scylfings first
sought out the Geats with savage intentions.
Early did Ohthere's age-laden father,
old and terrible, give a blow in return,
killing the sea-king; he rescued the queen-mother,
the old one's consort, deprived of her gold,
the mother of Onela and of Ohthere as well,
and then pursued the feud-nursing foemen until,
bereft of their ruler, they barely entered Ravenswood.
Then with vast-numbered forces he assaulted the remnant,
weary with wounds; he promised woe often,
the whole night long, to that sad-hearted war-troop:
he said at morning he would kill them with the edges of weapons,
some on the gallows for the glee of the fowls.
Aid came afterward to the anxious-in-spirit
at dawn of day, once they heard Higelac's bugle
and trumpet-sound, when that good one proceeded
and came following with the flower of the troopers.

chapters.title: Fitt XLI — The Messenger's Retrospect
paragraphs:
"The blood-stained trace of Swedes and Geats,
the death-rush of warmen, was widely noticed,
how the two peoples awakened the feud with each other.
The worthy one then went with well-beloved comrades,
old and dejected, to go to the fastness;
Ongentheow the earl turned upward then;
he had heard on inquiry of Higelac's battle,
of that exultant one's prowess, and despaired of being able
to resist, to struggle with the earls of the ocean,
to save his hoard-treasure against sea-going sailors,
his wife and his children; he fled from there afterward,
old, beneath the earth-wall. Then pursuit was offered
to the braves of the Swede-men, the banner to Higelac.
They fared then forth over the field-of-protection,
once the Hrethling heroes had thronged them to the hedge.
Then with edges of iron Ongentheow was driven,
the gray-haired, to turn at bay, so that the troop-ruler had
to suffer the power of Eofor alone:

Wulf then wildly assaulted him with weapon,
Wonred's son, so that from the swinge of the edges
the blood burst out in currents from his body,
forth beneath his hair. He was not afraid, however,
the gray-haired Scylfing, but speedily repaid

the wasting wound-stroke with a worse exchange,
when the king of the thane-troop turned thither:
the wise-minded son of Wonred was powerless
to give a return-blow to the age-hoary man,
but Ongentheow first hewed his head-shielding helmet to pieces,
so that, flecked with gore, he had to totter,
and fell to the earth; he was not yet doomed,
but sprang up again though an edge-wound had reached him.

Then Higelac's vassal, valiant and dauntless,
when his brother lay dead, made his broad-bladed weapon,
an ancient giant-sword, defense of the giants,
sweep over the shield-wall; the folk-prince succumbed then,

the shepherd of his people, was pierced to the vitals.
There were many attendants who bound up his kinsman,
carried him quickly when occasion was granted,
so that they were able to manage the place of the slain.
While this went on, one hero plundered the other,
ravished Ongentheow of his iron armor,
his hilted hard-sword and helmet together;

he carried the old one's equipments to Higelac.
Higelac received the jewels and graciously promised
rewards among the troopers, and so did he accomplish it:
the king of the Weders requited the war-rush,
Hrethel's descendant, when he returned home,

to Eofor and Wulf with wide-lavished treasures,
to each of them granting a hundred of thousands
in land and in rings wrought out of wire:

no man upon middle-earth needed to twit him
for the gifts he gave them, when they had conquered glory;

and to Eofor then he gave his one only daughter,
the honor of his home, as an earnest of favor.
That is the feud and the hatred — I expect it will come to pass —
the anger of earth-men, which the earls of the Swede-men
will visit on us, when they hear that our leader
lies lifeless, he who long protected
his hoard and his kingdom against hating assailers,
who, after the fall of the heroes, once defended
the deed-mighty Scyldings, did for the troopers
what best availed them, and accomplished, furthermore,

hero-deeds besides. Now haste is most fitting,
that we look upon the lord of liegemen yonder,
and carry that one to the death-pyre on his journey
who gave us ring-presents. Not any part of it
shall melt with the brave one — there is a mass of bright jewels,
gold beyond measure, grimly purchased,
and ending it all, ornament-rings likewise
bought with his life; these fire shall devour,
flame shall cover; no earl-man shall wear
a jewel-memento, nor shall any beautiful virgin
have on her neck rings to adorn her,
but, wretched in spirit, bereft of gold-gems,
she shall often with others be exiled and banished,
since the leader of liegemen has forsaken laughter,
mirth and merriment. Hence many a war-spear,
cold in the morning, shall be clutched in the fingers,
heaved in the hand; no harp-music's sound
shall waken the warriors, but the wan-coated raven,
eager over fey ones, shall gabble freely,
shall say to the eagle how he sped in the eating,
when, the wolf his companion, he plundered the slain."
So the high-minded hero was rehearsing these stories
loathsome to hear; he lied as to but few

of weirds and of words. All the war-troop arose then,
and beneath the Eagle's Cape sadly betook themselves,
weeping and woeful, to look on the wonder.
They saw on the sand then, lying soulless,
holding his slaughter-bed, him who had given them rings
in days that were done; then the death-bringing moment
had come to the good one, that the king very warlike,
Wielder of the Weders, had perished in a wondrous death.
First they beheld there a creature more wondrous,
the worm on the field, lying in front of them,
the foeman before them: the fire-spewing dragon,
ghostly and grisly guest in his terrors,
was scorched in the fire; as he lay there, he measured
fifty feet; he had come forth at night-time
to rejoice in the air, thereafter departing
to visit his den; he was now fastened in death,
he would rejoice in no other earth-hollowed caverns.
There stood round about him beakers and vessels,
dishes were lying and dear-valued weapons,
eaten with iron-rust, as if in earth's mighty bosom
a thousand winters they had there rested:

that mighty bequest was then guarded with magic,
the gold of the ancients, so that not any earl-man
could touch the ring-hall, save only Ruling-God,
the Sooth-king of Victories, who gave whom He wished

(He is earth-folk's protector) to open the treasure,
even to such among mortals as seemed to Him proper.

chapters.title: Fitt XLII — Wiglaf's Sad Story — The Hoard Carried Off
paragraphs:
Then it was seen that the journey had profited him little
who had wrongly hidden the ornaments within,
down beneath the wall. The warden had earlier slaughtered
a few of the folk-troop: the feud was then thereafter
hotly avenged. It is a wonder where,
when the strength-famous trooper has attained the end
of his allotted life-days, the man may no longer
remain with his kinsmen where mead-cups are flowing.
So it happened to Beowulf when he sought out the assaults
of the ward of the barrow: he himself had no knowledge
of how his leaving this life was likely to happen.
For until doomsday, the famous folk-leaders who placed it there
called it down with curses — that the man who ever ravaged this place
should be ever convicted of ill-deeds,
confined in foul places, fastened in hell-bonds,
punished with plagues. Beowulf cared not for gold:
rather he preferred to get first sight of the Wielder's favor.

Wiglaf spoke then, Wihstan's son:
"Often many an earl-man must endure sorrow
on account of one man, as has happened to us.
We could little prevail upon our beloved liegelord,
the kingdom's keeper, to follow counsel —
not to go to the guardian of the gold-hoard, but to let him
lie where he long was, live in his dwelling
until the end of the world. We met a destiny
hard to endure: the hoard has been looked upon,
been gained very grimly; too grievous the fate
that pricked the prince of the people to come thither.
I was inside and looked at all of it,
the building's equipments, once access was granted me —
by no means kindly was entrance permitted

within under the earth-wall. Hastily I seized
and held in my hands a huge-weighing burden
of costly hoard-treasures, and bore them out hither
to my beloved liegelord: life was yet in him,
and consciousness also; the old one discoursed then
much and mournfully, commanded me to greet you,

bade that, remembering the deeds of your friend-lord,
you build on the fire-hill of corpses a lofty
burial-barrow, broad and far-famous,
as he was most widely honored among world-dwelling warriors
while he reveled in riches. Let us rouse ourselves and hasten
again to see and to seek out the treasure,
the wonder beneath the wall. The way I will show you,
so that you may look closely at ring-gems sufficient
and gold in abundance. Let the bier be fashioned
promptly and fully, when we come forth again,
and let us lift our lord then, to where he shall long tarry,
the well-beloved warrior, beneath the Wielder's protection."

Then the son of Wihstan, the mood-valiant man,
bade orders be given to many of the heroes,
holders of homesteads, that they from far away,
as leaders of liegemen, should seek out the good one
with wood for his pyre: "The flame shall now swallow
(the wan fire shall wax) the warriors' leader,
he who often withstood the rain of the iron,
when, sturdily hurled, the storm of the arrows
leapt over the linden-wall, and the lance gave service,
with the arrow, furnished with feathers, following after."
Now the wise-minded son of Wihstan summoned
the best of the braves from the ruler's band,

seven together; beneath the enemy's roof he
went with the seven; one of the heroes
who fared at the front bore in his hand
a fire-blazing torchlight. No lot then decided
who should havoc that hoard, when the hero-earls saw it
lying in the cavern uncared-for entirely,
rusting to ruin: they rued then but little
that they hastily hauled out the treasure,

the dear-valued jewels; the dragon also they pushed,
the worm over the wall, let the wave-currents take him,
the waters enwind the ward of the treasures.

There wounden gold was loaded onto a wain,
a mass unmeasured; the men-leader then,
the hoary hero, was carried off to Whale's-Ness.

chapters.title: Fitt XLIII — The Burning of Beowulf
paragraphs:
The folk of the Geats got ready for him then
a pile on the earth, strong for the burning,
hung about with helmets, hero-knights' targes,
and bright-shining byrnies, as he had begged they should have;
then the wailing war-heroes laid in the middle
their world-famous chieftain, their beloved liegelord.

Soldiers then began to kindle upon the barrow
the largest of dead-fires: dark above the vapor
the smoke-cloud ascended, the sad-roaring fire,
mingled with weeping (the wind-roar subsided)
until the building of bone it had broken to pieces,
hot at the heart. Heavy in spirit,
mood-sad, they lamented the men-leader's ruin;
and the much-grieving widow sang mournful measures

The men of the Weders accordingly made
a hill on the height, high and extensive,
to be seen from afar by sea-going sailors,
and built the brave one's beacon where the fire had been,
in the space of ten days, surrounded it with a wall,
as the wisest of world-folk could most worthily plan it.
They placed in the barrow rings and jewels,

all such ornaments as, earlier, war-minded men
had won into their possession out of the treasure:
the earnings of earl-men they entrusted to the earth,
the gold to the dust, where it yet remains
as useless to mortals as in ages before.
Then around the death-mound rode the doughty-in-battle,
sons of all twelve of the chiefs of the people;
they would mourn further, lament for their ruler,
speak in measure, mention him with pleasure,
weigh his worth and his warlike achievements,
mightily commend them, as it is meet one praise
his liegelord in words and love him in spirit,
when he fares forth from his body to destruction.
So the men of the Geats, mourning, lamented
the fall of their lord, his fond-loving vassals,

and said he was the kindest of kings under heaven,
the gentlest of men, the most winning of manner,
the friendliest to folk-troops, and the fondest of honor.
